about: ScanRuler for FreeCAD's tools for agents (through Agent Link, in its tool-data format): name, what it does, its arguments as JSON Schema, its group, whether it changes the document. The handlers are scanrulerfc/handlers; ported from ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen).

scan_open.description: Open a 3D scan to measure, in place of the one open. Inputs: path or object, one of them. path: STL, PLY, OBJ, OFF or 3MF through FreeCAD's Mesh module. path can also be glTF/GLB, Collada, VRML or 3DS through Agent Link's readers, in the units that their format says. object: a mesh in the document, by label or name, taken as millimetres. object must be a mesh only: mesh a solid first with meshobj_from_shape. units: mm (default), cm, m or in, for a file. discard: true is needed to replace a scan that has elements or dimensions on it; they go with it. What it does in FreeCAD: the scan is put in the document as its own mesh object. The Placement of that object follows the alignment. A document mesh that it was read from is hidden, not deleted: shownAs says so. ScanRuler's state is kept in the document, so FreeCAD's Save carries it. Gotchas: a mesh exported from CAD has vertices only on its edges. scan_qa then says tessellation.sparse; mesh_densify cures it before fits, segmentation and section fits. A wrong unit shows as a size warning. Open again with units, or use scan_scale, to cure it. Refused: a file over 1 GB, or a scan over 20,000,000 triangles. A 3MF that is a ZIP bomb is refused before it is read. Size: the scan is read whole into memory, on FreeCAD's own thread. So the window waits, and it cannot run as a job. Past 2,000,000 triangles, every tool grows slow; the answer warns: mesh_reduce first. Reading time is not measured. The answer holds: opened { file, units, vertices, triangles, box { min, max, size }, centre, area mm² }, shownAs, and warnings. warnings: a scan under 1 mm or over 5 m across, and the triangle count. warnings also names vertices that were not numbers, dropped with their triangles. Read the warnings before you measure.
scan_open.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/scan.py

scan_nearest.description: Find where a place lands on the scan. Input at: { vertex: n } (numbered from 0) or { point: [x, y, z] }. The point is in mm, in the frame that the scan is measured in now. A point snaps to the nearest vertex, not to the nearest place on a triangle. Use it to check that a point lies on the surface meant, before you fit there. Use it also to turn coordinates into a vertex number. The answer holds: vertex, point (its coordinates), normal (outward), triangle and distance. triangle: the three vertices of one triangle that it is a corner of. distance: mm, from the point asked about. A large distance means that the point is off the part, or that the frame is not the one assumed. An alignment moves every coordinate. On a sparse CAD tessellation, the nearest vertex can be far along a face: mesh_densify first. It reads the vertices once (0.9 s at 68,000 vertices, measured in plain Python off the Mac). Changes nothing.

point.description: A point, mm; the nearest vertex is taken.

scan_nearest.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/scan.py

scan_query.description: Get the vertices of the scan inside a box, or within a radius of a point, with their outward normals. These are the points on a face. Inputs: box { min, max } or near { at, radius }, one of them (mm, current frame). normal { dir, withinDeg (30) } keeps only those facing that way. limit: 1000; 20000 at most. fields: count, ids or all. count: the numbers alone; the default with mark. ids: with vertex numbers. all: with points and normals; the default. mark: true leaves every matching vertex marked for element_fit_marked { marked: true }. Gotcha: at most limit come back, every k-th, spread evenly, and step says k. But matched counts them all, and mark marks them all, not the thinned list. A box that reaches a neighbouring face takes its vertices too (the walls of a pocket beside a top face). Keep the box tight, or add normal. The answer holds: matched, returned, step, bounds { min, max }, centroid, meanNormal, marked { points, from }, vertices, points, normals. An empty answer (matched 0) usually means the wrong frame: scan_info gives the box. Changes nothing on the part.

box.description: A box in the current frame.

fields.description: count: the numbers alone (the default with mark); ids: with the vertices; all: with points and normals (the default).

limit.description: How many vertices at most; 1000 by default, 20000 at most.

mark.description: Leave every matching vertex marked, for element_fit_marked { marked: true }.

near.description: A ball about a point, in place of box.

normal.description: Only the vertices whose outward normal faces this way.

scan_segment.description: Find the planar regions of the scan, all at once (ScanRuler's vertex method). Regions grow from the flattest places outward, within maxDeg (15°) and maxRms (0.05 mm). Regions smaller than minArea are given back. minArea: a square with a side of 2 % of the diagonal of the scan. On a sparse mesh, that finds nothing. A sparse mesh is a CAD-style tessellation. For example, a cylinder cap is a fan of triangles with vertices only on its rim. Then the triangles are grouped instead (the faces method). Triangles in one plane are a plane. A smooth strip of faces square to one axis, with corners on a cylinder within maxRms, is a cylinder. Inputs: method auto (default), vertices or faces. auto runs vertices, then faces only when that found nothing and the mesh is sparse. box { min, max } confines it. limit (20, 200 at most) is how many regions are listed. mark: the id of a region, or several, leaves their points marked for element_fit_marked { marked: true }. list: true gives the regions too. Gotchas: region ids are of the settings of this call, so mark with the same settings. On a densified CAD mesh, a round wall comes back as its flat facets (one narrow plane each). So count the large regions only. area is of the points gathered, a little under the area of the face. The answer holds: found, method (which ran), why (when faces ran under auto), considered, claimed, shown and regions. regions, largest first: id, kind, sigma, area mm², box, vertices, neighbours { id, deg }. kind plane: normal, point; kind cylinder: axis, point, radius, length, bore. Size: it reads every vertex. It is declared heavy, so on its own it runs as a job (job_status gives the answer past 45 s). Measured 1.2 s at 137,000 triangles in plain Python off the Mac; the Mac is not measured. The result is kept until the scan moves. Changes nothing.

box.description: A box in the current frame.

kind.description: What to find; plane, the default and for now the only one asked for (the faces method also reports the cylinders it finds).

limit.description: How many regions are listed; 20 by default.

list.description: With mark: the list of regions too.

mark.description: Leave this region's points marked, or several regions'.

method.description: auto (the default): ScanRuler's vertex growing, and the triangle grouping only when that finds nothing on a sparse mesh; vertices: ScanRuler's alone; faces: the triangle grouping alone (a CAD mesh whose flats the vertex method misses beside finely tessellated curves).

minArea.description: mm²; by default a square 2 % of the scan's diagonal on a side.

scan_segment.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/scan.py

scan_fit_surface.description: Measure a patch of the scan as a surface: a sloped side, a twisted ruled face, a dome, a saddle. Inputs: vertices (7 or more vertex numbers) or box { min, max } (mm), one of them. normal { dir, withinDeg } keeps only what faces a way. model: plane, bilinear, quadric or best. best (default) fits each model and names the simplest whose rms is within a tenth of the lowest. limit: 20000 points at most, spread evenly. The answer holds: points, frame { origin, basisU, basisV, normal } and models. Each model is a height over (u, v) in that frame. plane: a + b·u + c·v. bilinear: + d·u·v. quadric: + d·u² + e·u·v + f·v², with curvature { k1, k2 (1/mm), r1, r2 (mm, null when flat), axis1, axis2, shape }. Each model has coefficients, rms and worst (mm); best names the model. Gotchas: heights are in the own frame of the patch, not world z. A box that takes in a neighbouring face fits a bend that is not there. For a plane, sphere, cylinder, cone or torus, use element_fit, which keeps an element. Refused: under 7 points, or points that lie on a line. Changes nothing, keeps nothing.

box.description: A box in the current frame.

limit.description: How many points at most; 20000 by default.

model.description: Which surface; best (the default) fits each and names the simplest that holds.

normal.description: Only the vertices whose outward normal faces this way.

vertices.description: The scan vertices of the patch.

scan_qa.description: Make one call before modelling, to know what the scan will and will not give. Input: axis (x, y, z or a direction) for the thickness reading. By default, axis is the z of the alignment, or unaligned, the way most of the surface faces. The answer holds: rims, noise, tessellation, sheet, thickness and notes. rims: the open edges of its holes. rims holds count, total length, and the largest with rim number, at, size and circle { center, axis, diameter } where one fits. noise { median, p90, sampled }: mm scatter of small plane fits. noise is 0 on a CAD tessellation, with measured: the bends between facets. tessellation { cad, sparse, spacing, flatShare, densifyTo }: when the mesh was exported from CAD. sparse: true means mesh_densify { maxEdge: densifyTo } before any fit, segmentation or section fit. sheet { gauge { p5, p50, p95 }, twoSkins, reach }: where most of the area has a second skin facing back. sheet holds apart too: tabs, ribs and bosses standing off the walls. thickness { axis, axisFrom, cells, p5, p50, p95, tiltDeg, run, over, faces { topDeg, bottomDeg } }: through the part along axis. notes: what looks wrong, in plain words; read them all. Gotchas: a scanned skin with no rims, or only pinholes, is a wrap. A wrap bridged the holes that it did not see through: read each hole from both ends. On a sheet or thin shell, thickness reads the box across the part; the wall is sheet.gauge. A tiltDeg of 0.2° or more is a merge error or a real taper. Settle it before you model to one thickness. Size: it reads every triangle (rims, and a ray grid through the part). Measured 1.7 s at 219,000 triangles in a Linux container, since the rays walk a grid (7.3 s before). The Mac is not measured. It is declared heavy, so on its own it runs as a job. job_status gives the answer past 45 s. Changes nothing.

scan_draft.description: Gather into patches the walls of the scan that run near a pull direction. These are the sides that a mould opens along. Each patch has draftDeg, the angle that it leans off the pull. draftDeg is positive where the wall faces partly along the pull. It is negative where the wall faces back: a back draft, an undercut. Inputs: pull [x, y, z] (needed, any length). box { min, max }. nearDeg (10): how far off square to the pull a wall may lean and count; 45 at most. patches: 12, the largest first; 100 at most. minArea: 1 mm². split: a plane that no patch reaches across: "symmetry", a plane element, "XY", "YZ", "XZ" or { point, normal }. The answer holds: pull, nearDeg, points, walls (points on walls), found, split, and patches. patches: draftDeg, sigmaDeg (of the mean), spreadDeg, area mm², count, centroid, box, facing, turnDeg, round, side. round: the round side of a boss or hole. Gotchas: read it early on a moulded or cast part, along each direction that the tools open. Walls that lean half a degree to a few degrees explain fits that miss by the lean. Patches grow between neighbouring points by the median point spacing, and area is count × spacing². On an unevenly sampled mesh, walls break into strips or drop out, and areas read small. Examples: a densified CAD tessellation, or rows of vertices far apart. Trust it on a real, evenly sampled scan. Size: over 400,000 vertices, every k-th is read. 0.3 s at 68,000 vertices (plain Python off the Mac). Changes nothing.

box.description: A box in the current frame.

nearDeg.description: Degrees off square to the pull a wall may lean and count; 10 by default.

patches.description: How many patches, the largest first; 12 by default.

split.description: A plane no patch reaches across.

scan_pattern.description: Count rotational repeats about an axis from the scan. Examples: the blades of a fan, the holes of a flange, spokes, gear teeth. The scan is cut square to the axis at each height, and each cut is turned against itself. Inputs: axis (needed): a cylinder, cone, line or circle element by id or name. axis can also be "X", "Y", "Z" (through the zero of the frame), or { origin, dir }. at: heights along the axis in mm, from the foot of the zero point on it. By default, at is six heights spread over the part; 12 at most. radius { min, max } keeps only the outline between those radii. Use radius to leave out a housing that does not repeat. count (60): the most copies looked for. instances: false leaves the figures of each copy out. The answer holds: axis { name, origin, dir, zeroDir } and heights. Each height: count, pitchDeg, phaseDeg (from zeroDir), betweenDeg, score (0 to 1), rms, worst, worstInstance, length, instances, rings. length: mm of outline read. instances { angleDeg, radius, offDeg, rms, worst, share }: a copy out of place or worn reads off. rings { radius, off, towardDeg, rms }: the round outlines about the axis. Gotchas: count 1 with tried { count, score } means that no repeat held (score under 0.5). tried is only the best guess, not a finding. A count that changes between heights is two features, so narrow with at and radius. A few cuts of the mesh: 0.3 s at 137,000 triangles (plain Python off the Mac). Changes nothing.

axis.description: The axis the pattern turns about.

count.description: The most copies looked for; 60 by default.

instances.description: Each copy's figures; true by default.

radius.description: Only the outline between these radii.

scan_heightmap.description: Find where the scan is first met over a grid of cells. It looks along an axis, or square onto a plane. In one call it reads pocket floors, ledges and the height of a step. It also reads the tilt of a face, the tiers of a pad, or an icon on a key. Inputs: axis or plane, one of them. axis: -z by default (the top from above); ±x, ±y, ±z. plane: a plane element, "XY", "YZ", "XZ" or { origin, normal, u? }. flip looks from the other side of the plane. box limits it. With axis, box is { min, max } in mm. With plane, box is [u, v, height] in the frame of the plane, or { world: { min, max } }. cell: mm. cell is widened to keep 1,600 cells with the grid, 25,600 without; note says so. of: height (default), deviation or relief. deviation: the reading of the deviation map where each ray lands; it needs a map. relief: height less the surface round it, for icons, grooves, lettering. smooth: mm, three cells by default. levels: true gathers the values into levels in place of the grid. gap: the least gap between two levels, mm. slopeDeg (10): steeper cells are left out of the levels of a height. grid: false and picture: true write the map as a PNG (path, or in the folder of the session). The answer holds: axis or plane (its frame), along, across, of, cell, origin [u0, v0], cols, rows, hit, valued, min, max. grid: rows from the low v up, null where nothing is met. grid[r][c] stands at u0 + (c + ½)·cell, v0 + (r + ½)·cell. levels, largest first: height, sigma, range, cells, area mm², sharePct, box. For a height of 5 % or more, a level also holds plane { origin, normal }. align_datum { primary: { plane } } levels on that plane. warp { rise, bow, note }: when a gentle warp was taken out first. ramps: where slopes join tiers. scanLies: when few cells meet the scan. picture { path, note }. Gotchas: a through hole reads null, not a depth. The area of a level counts whole cells, so it runs under the area of the face. With plane, heights are along its normal from its origin, not world z. Size: on the first call after the scan changes, every triangle goes into a search structure. Then rays are cast. 5 s the first time and 1.5 s after, at 137,000 triangles. That is plain Python off the Mac; the Mac is not measured. Declared heavy: on its own it runs as a job. Changes nothing in the document.

scan_outline.description: Read the outline of the scan as a sketch would draw it. It is seen along an axis, or square onto a plane. Examples: the plan of a flange, the opening of a bezel, the shape of a gasket. Each loop becomes the fewest lines and arcs that follow it within tolerance. A round loop becomes one circle. Inputs: axis, plane, flip and box, as scan_heightmap takes them (u, v as it lays them). tolerance: mm (0.2). loops: 4, the largest first; 50 at most. The answer holds: axis or plane, across, cell, tolerance, and loops. loops: hole (true for an opening seen right through), area mm², box, then circle or points. circle { center, radius, rms }. points: [u, v] corners in order, with rounds and arcs. rounds { at, radius, center }: a rounded corner at points[at]. arcs { from, radius, center, mid }: from points[from] through mid to the next point. worst: mm that the trace strays from what is drawn; worstAt when past the tolerance. more counts the loops not listed. Gotchas: this is the shadow of everything along the view, not a cut. A pocket that does not go through leaves no loop; section_cut cuts at a height. Only what is seen through counts as a hole. The cell is half the tolerance, and it is widened past 250,000 cells. note then says to what: give a box round the part looked for, to read it finer. To get a sketch, use section_cut { kind: "shadow" }, then section_to_sketch. 0.6 s at 137,000 triangles (plain Python off the Mac). Changes nothing.

scan_cloud.description: Write the scan as a point cloud file. It holds every vertex with its outward normal, mm. The pose is the one that the scan is measured in now (after any alignment or scale). Inputs: format ply (default) or xyz. ply: binary little-endian, float x y z nx ny nz. xyz: text, a line each: x y z nx ny nz. path: a relative name goes in the folder of the session. Left out, path is <scan>-cloud.<format> there. The answer holds: file { path, name, bytes }, points, format, note. Size: one record a vertex: 24 bytes in PLY, about 50 in XYZ (3.5 MB for 68,000 vertices). Vertices only: triangles are not written (mesh_export writes the mesh). Changes nothing in the document.
scan_cloud.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/scan.py

scan_info.description: Read the scan that is open, in the frame that it is measured in now. The answer holds: scan { file, units, vertices, triangles, box { min, max, size }, centre, area mm² }, and how many elements and dimensions are on it. No inputs. With no scan open, it answers scan: null and a note, not a refusal. Call it after scan_open, an alignment or scan_scale, to learn where the coordinates now lie. Every place given to the other tools is in this frame. After ScanRuler's state is written into the document, it also answers kept { bytes, ms, arrays, packedAgain }. bytes and ms: the size and time of the last write of that state (the copy that FreeCAD's Save carries). arrays: how many arrays it holds. packedAgain: how many of them had changed and were compressed again for that write. Some calls change no mesh: a rename, a dimension, a limit. After such a call, packedAgain is 0 or a few small ones. ms is then a few tens. A large packedAgain or ms on such a call is worth reporting. Changes nothing.
scan_info.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/scan.py

element_fit.description: Fit an element on the scan and keep it. kind (needed): plane, sphere, cylinder, cone, torus, point or circle. A plane, sphere, cylinder, cone or torus grows its surface from the place or places in at. Then it is best-fitted to that surface. The fit is a robust first estimate, region growing, then a Gaussian best fit with a sigma cut-off. point is the place itself. circle goes through three or more places. Inputs: at: a place { vertex } or { point: [x, y, z] }, or a list of them. A point is in mm, in the current frame; the nearest vertex is taken. name. sigma: 3 (default), 2, 1 or 0 (no cut-off). mark: true leaves the grown region marked for element_fit_marked. To say what is sought, give side, radius, axis or within. side: inside (a bore) or outside (a shaft). radius { min, max }. axis: for a cylinder or cone, roughly, within 20°. within { min, max }: the surface stays in this box. knownDiameter: for a sphere, the diameter of a gauge ball is held, and the centre alone is fitted. assumed: for a sphere or cylinder, the designed diameter, kept beside the fit. Gotchas: a seed near an edge can land on the neighbouring surface. The seeds (inRegion, offMm, deg) and warning of the answer say so. side, radius, axis or within pass over what does not match. A circle through exactly three places has sigma and formError null. Under six places, the form of a circle is not to be judged. On a CAD tessellation, fit only after mesh_densify. A polygonal bore reads a hair under its true diameter (the chords of its facets). The region of a plane stops at the edges of the face. So its centre is the centre of the region, not of the face. The answer holds: element { id, name, kind, fit, source }, with seeds and region { area, box }. fit holds { center and normal (plane), axis, radius, length, coverage° (round ones), sigma (RMS, mm), formError (peak to peak), residualMin / Max, usedPoints of regionSize }. Later calls take the element by id or name. Refused: no surface of that kind is found there; the message says what to try. 0.2 s or less on a 137,000-triangle scan (plain Python off the Mac). It changes ScanRuler's state in the document (one undo step), not the shapes of the model. element_to_document makes it geometry.

element_fit_marked.description: Fit a plane, sphere, cylinder, cone or torus to exactly the scan vertices given, with no search for the surface. Use it when the growing of element_fit takes too much or too little. Inputs: kind (needed), and vertices, marked or box, one of them. vertices: three or more vertex numbers. marked: true takes the points that the last mark left marked. The marks come from element_fit { mark: true }, scan_segment { mark } or scan_query { mark: true }. box { min, max }, with normal { dir, withinDeg } to keep only what faces a way. normal goes with box only. name, sigma, knownDiameter and assumed: as element_fit. Gotchas: every point given is fitted, so strays in the box bend the fit. The sigma cut-off (3 by default) drops outliers from the fit. But a form tolerance on the element (dimension_add form-flatness …) is read over every point given, strays included. The next call that marks replaces the marked points. The answer holds: element (as element_fit: fit with sigma, formError, usedPoints of regionSize; source.markedPoints). With box, it also holds how many points it took. Refused: nothing is marked. Refused: the box holds too few points. Refused: the points do not span the surface asked for. It changes ScanRuler's state in the document, not the model.

element_construct.description: Construct an element from others and from typed-in numbers. kind and method are needed. point: point-coords, point-centroid, point-midpoint, point-line-plane, point-center, point-three-planes, point-line-line, point-project. line: line-two-points, line-axis, line-plane-plane, line-plane-point, line-project, line-coords. plane: plane-three-points, plane-offset, plane-midplane, plane-offset-point, plane-line-point, plane-angle, plane-line-plane, plane-two-lines, plane-tangent-sphere, plane-tangent-cylinder, plane-coords, plane-symmetry. circle: circle-plane-cylinder, circle-plane-sphere, circle-coords. Inputs: refs fill the slots of the method in order, by id or name. In a plane slot, "XY", "YZ", "XZ" become plane elements, listed under made. params: the numbers of the method, in order or by key, in mm and degrees. The keys: [x, y, z; offset; angle; gap; nx, ny, nz, px, py, pz; dx, dy, dz, length; d, cx, cy, cz]. name. vertices confines point-centroid and plane-symmetry to those scan vertices. seed: the plane that plane-symmetry starts its search from. Gotchas: a constructed element follows its sources. It moves when they are fitted again, and it goes when one is removed (element_unlink freezes it). It has no measured surface, so form tolerances refuse it. A wrong count or kind of refs is refused, with the slots that the method takes. plane-symmetry searches the scan (4,000 sampled points) and answers symmetry { rms, matched, sampled, note }. A mirror RMS past about 0.1 mm is not a symmetry to build on. The RMS is of the matched samples only. matched under sampled means that the plane mirrors most of the part, not all of it. An example is a pocket or boss on one side alone; note says so. Such a plane can be taken before the exact mirror plane of the part. This is most likely on a noise-free CAD tessellation. So where the part should have one, give seed ("XY", "XZ", "YZ" or a plane element), and compare matched. The answer holds: element { id, name, kind, fit, source { method, refs, params } }, made. It changes ScanRuler's state in the document, not the model.

assumed.description: The designed diameter, mm: kept beside the fit, reported as measured.

element_rename.description: Give an element another name. Inputs: element (id or name), name. Dimensions and constructions on it keep pointing at it; they hold its id. Gotcha: names are matched without regard to case. Two elements with one name can afterwards be told apart only by id. Choose a name that is not in use (element_list). The answer holds the element. It changes ScanRuler's state in the document.

element_unlink.description: Freeze a constructed point, line, plane or circle where it stands. Its sources give way to coordinates of its own (point-coords, line-coords, plane-coords, circle-coords). So it no longer moves when they do, and it stays if they are removed. Input: element (id or name). Refused: an element not built from others (a fitted one has nothing to unlink). Refused: a constructed kind with no coordinates form. No tool undoes it: construct it again to link it. The answer holds the element with its new source. It changes ScanRuler's state in the document.
element_unlink.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/elements.py

element_remove.description: Delete an element. With it go every construction built on it, and every dimension on any of them. The deviation map against it also goes, when it was the deviation target. deviationTargetCleared: the map falls back to the map of the reference part. Input: element (id or name). Gotcha: the cascade is not asked about. element_list shows the source.refs of each element first, and element_unlink keeps a construction that should stay. The answer holds: removed [{ id, name }] (the element and the constructions that went with it), dimensionsRemoved [{ id, name }], deviationTargetCleared. No tool brings them back: fit or construct again. It changes ScanRuler's state in the document, not the model.

element_set_visible.description: Show or hide one element, or all of them. Inputs: visible (needed: true or false), and element (id or name) or all: true. A hidden element still measures and still carries its dimensions. The flag is kept for the report and the views. The answer holds: element { id, name, visible }, or with all: elements [{ id, name, visible }]. It changes ScanRuler's state in the document.
element_set_visible.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/elements.py

element_list.description: List the elements on the scan, each with its fit and how it came about. Each holds: id, name, kind, status, visible, fit and source. fit: center, normal or axis, radius, sigma, formError, usedPoints of regionSize …. source: for fitted, method, cut-off, seeds; for constructed, method, refs, params; for picked, points. No inputs. Coordinates are in the frame that the scan is measured in now. The answer grows with the count (about 0.5 kB an element). With many, read report_get { format: "text" } instead. Changes nothing.

align_datum.description: Make a 3-2-1 alignment: move the scan, and everything measured on it, into the own coordinates of the part. Inputs: primary levels the part: { element } (a plane), { points: 3 points } or { plane: { origin, normal } }. The outward normal of primary becomes primaryAxis. primaryAxis is z- by default: a base plane faces down, and the part stands on z = 0. secondary turns it about that normal: { element } (a line, an axis, or a plane) or { points: 2 points }. secondary is laid along secondaryAxis (x+ by default). origin is the zero point: { element } (a point, sphere, circle or torus) or { point }. keepFree: true. Axes are x+, x-, y+, y-, z+, z-. Gotchas: a plane as secondary puts its outward NORMAL on secondaryAxis, not its direction along the part. Each datum zeroes the coordinates that it owns, and the origin zeroes only those left open. An origin alone moves without turning; secondary needs primary. On a first alignment, the coordinates that nothing sets are centred on the box of the scan, unless keepFree. Every coordinate given to other tools afterwards is in the new frame (scan_info gives the box). It drops a deviation alignment and its map (deviation_align again). In FreeCAD, the mesh object of the scan gets the alignment as its Placement. A move made on that object in the window is carried back into the scan before the next call. The answer holds: applied { rotation, translation, rotationDeg, moveMm }, elements (how many moved), sections, centred, origin { set, at, note } and parallelFace. sections: how many sections moved with the part, when any. parallelFace: when a face parallel to the levelling plane holds more of the scan. align_clear undoes it. It changes ScanRuler's state and the Placement of the scan object, not the model. When the scan moved, the answer also holds timing { ms, object, mesh }. ms: the own work of the tool. object: the part of ms spent writing the mesh object of the scan in the FreeCAD document. mesh: "kept" (the Placement of the object only) or "rebuilt" (every vertex written again: scan_scale). ms does not hold the state kept in the document, written after the answer. The kept of scan_info says what that cost. ms does not hold what the host does round the call.

align_auto.description: Read a coordinate system off the scan and apply it (ScanRuler's Auto-align). It finds the directions that most faces are square to, and the axis that round walls run along. The part stands on its base. The base is its largest flat face, or the side that an open scan is open on. Or the base is an end of its main axis. Its long side goes along X. Zero goes under the middle, on the base (on the axis for a turned part). Input: level settled (default) or largest. settled: all faces laid on the axes at once, by area. largest: the largest flat face squared exactly, and the rest settled about its normal. Gotchas: a drafted wall reads as its draft, not as an alignment error (square.axes lists the tilt of each face). It chooses which way is +X and which face is the base. When the datums of the drawing matter, use align_datum. It moves every coordinate (scan_info after), and it drops a deviation alignment and its map. The answer holds: applied { rotation, translation, rotationDeg, moveMm }, note, method planes | axis | principal, base, planeShare, wallShare, square { largest, axes [{ axis, tiltDeg, area, faces }] }, largestInside, elements, sections. note: what it was read from, in words. largestInside: when that face looks into the part. elements: how many moved; sections: how many sections moved with it, when any. It reads every vertex: 0.7 s at 137,000 triangles (plain Python off the Mac). Refused: no direction can be read. align_clear undoes it. It changes ScanRuler's state and the Placement of the scan object, not the model. When the scan moved, the answer also holds timing { ms, object, mesh }. ms: the own work of the tool. object: the part of ms spent writing the mesh object of the scan in the FreeCAD document. mesh: "kept" (the Placement of the object only) or "rebuilt" (every vertex written again: scan_scale). ms does not hold the state kept in the document, written after the answer. The kept of scan_info says what that cost. ms does not hold what the host does round the call.

level.description: settled (the default): all faces at once, by area. largest: the largest flat face exactly, the rest settled about its normal.

align_auto.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/align.py

align_symmetry.description: Settle the pose of the part on its mirror plane, and apply it. The plane is the newest measured symmetry plane (element_construct plane-symmetry), or one searched for on the scan. The axis of the current frame nearest its normal is turned onto it. The zero point is put on the plane. The other two directions stay as they were. So align first (align_auto or align_datum), and call this to centre. No inputs. Refused: the scan has no symmetry plane; the message gives the figures. That is: the best mirror image stands over 0.5 mm off the scan (RMS). Or: under half the samples find their mirror image. Gotchas: a measured symmetry plane is used even when it is hidden. It is used even when it mirrors the part only nearly. For example, a block with a pocket in its top mirrors at mid-height, but for the pocket. Read symmetry.matchedShare. Make the plane meant with element_construct plane-symmetry and seed first. A part with two mirror planes settles on the one found first. Wear or damage on one half shifts the plane toward it. It drops a deviation alignment and its map. The answer holds: note, symmetry { rms, matchedShare, from }, applied (this move), appliedAlignment, elements. note: which plane, the mirror RMS, and how far it turned and moved. Some samples can have no mirror image about the plane. note then says that it is not a mirror of the whole part, and what share has none. from: the name of the element, or "search". appliedAlignment: the whole alignment since the scan was opened. 0.7 s at 137,000 triangles (plain Python off the Mac). align_clear undoes every alignment. It changes ScanRuler's state and the Placement of the scan object. When the scan moved, the answer also holds timing { ms, object, mesh }. ms: the own work of the tool. object: the part of ms spent writing the mesh object of the scan in the FreeCAD document. mesh: "kept" (the Placement of the object only) or "rebuilt" (every vertex written again: scan_scale). ms does not hold the state kept in the document, written after the answer. The kept of scan_info says what that cost. ms does not hold what the host does round the call.
align_symmetry.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/align.py

align_clear.description: Put the part back in the coordinates that the scanner delivered it in, with everything measured on it. Every alignment since scan_open is taken off at once; a scan_scale stays. No inputs. Refused (invalid_state): the part is in scan coordinates already. It drops a deviation alignment and its map, as every move does. The answer holds: appliedAlignment: null, elements (how many moved back) and sections (how many sections moved back, when any). It changes ScanRuler's state and the Placement of the scan object. When the scan moved, the answer also holds timing { ms, object, mesh }. ms: the own work of the tool. object: the part of ms spent writing the mesh object of the scan in the FreeCAD document. mesh: "kept" (the Placement of the object only) or "rebuilt" (every vertex written again: scan_scale). ms does not hold the state kept in the document, written after the answer. The kept of scan_info says what that cost. ms does not hold what the host does round the call.
align_clear.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/align.py

scan_scale.description: Scale the scan to its true size. A photogrammetry scan has no size of its own. A file read in the wrong unit is off by 10, 25.4 or 1000. Inputs: factor or references, one of them. factor: a number (25.4 for inches read as mm). references: lengths known two ways, each with true (mm on the real part). A reference is { dimension } (a distance or diameter dimension), { element } (a sphere, cylinder or circle: its diameter) or { points: two points }. dryRun: true works the factor out and scales nothing. Several references are averaged by length. The own factor and offPct of each come back, so a bad one shows. offPct: how far it is off the average. A spread over a per cent or so means that a reference is wrong, not that the average is right. Gotchas: the scale is about the zero point of the frame, so coordinates change (scan_info after). Elements and dimensions scale with it. Factors multiply; they do not replace (scale by 1/factor to go back). An alignment made with align_datum, align_auto or align_symmetry stays. Its move is scaled with the part, and align_clear still takes it off. It drops a deviation alignment and its map. In FreeCAD, the mesh object of the scan is rebuilt at the new size. This runs on the own thread of the window. That is slow on a large scan: 4.4 and 4.9 s at 219,600 triangles on the Mac, run 3. timing says how much of a call it was. A wall-thickness map taken before the scale is of the unscaled part, and it is dropped (thickness_measure again). The answer holds: factor, references [{ label, measured, true, factor, offPct }], spreadPct (with several), size { before, after } (the box diagonal, mm), dryRun. When scaled, it also holds scan (its summary), sections and timing { ms, object, mesh }. sections: how many sections were scaled with it, when any. ms: the own work of the tool. object: the part of ms spent writing the mesh object of the scan in the FreeCAD document. That is the new mesh and its Placement. mesh: "rebuilt". ms does not hold the state kept in the document, written after the answer. The kept of scan_info says what that cost. ms does not hold what the host does round the call. A document copy that an add-on makes after a change shows in the around row of Agent Link, not here. It changes ScanRuler's state and the mesh object of the scan.

points.description: The two ends of the length.

dimension_add.description: Measure between elements, or a size or tolerance of one, and keep it. Inputs: refs (needed): one to three elements by id or name, in slot order. type: left out, it follows the elements as clicking them does. Examples: two planes give their distance; a plane and an axis give theirs. Two spheres give the centre distance; a point and a cylinder give point to axis. Else type is one of [dist-point-point, dist-point-axis, dist-point-plane, dist-axis-axis, dist-axis-plane, dist-plane-plane, angle-axis-axis, angle-axis-plane, angle-plane-plane, size-diameter, form-flatness, form-cylindricity, form-circularity, form-sphericity, orient-parallelism, orient-perpendicularity, orient-angularity, loc-coaxiality]. name. anchor, for two spheres: center (default), gap or span. basic: the basic angle of an angularity, degrees. limit, for a verdict: { kind: "max", max } (a ceiling) or { kind: "band", nominal, plus, minus }. In a band, plus and minus are both positive; kind is needed. Gotchas: a signed distance (axis to plane, point to plane) is negative on the inner side of the plane. Judge it with a band about the signed value, or read its size. The distance of two planes is taken at the centre of the first plane. A warning comes when the patches do not overlap. A form or orientation tolerance is read as a minimum zone over every point of the region of the element. That includes points that the sigma cut-off of the fit dropped, so one stray vertex sets it. A constructed element has no surface, and form tolerances refuse it. These are GD&T-like readings off fitted elements of a noisy scan, not a certified inspection. The answer holds: dimension { id, name, type, family dimension | tolerance, title, refs, label, value (mm or degrees), unit, display, limit, verdict { pass, deviation, over, allowance, alarm }, detail, range, warning }. Refused: the elements do not seat in the type; the message names its slots. It changes ScanRuler's state in the document.

In a band, plus and minus are positive, in mm or degrees. The answer holds the dimension with verdict { pass, deviation, over, allowance, alarm }. deviation: from the nominal, or over the ceiling. over: how far past the allowance; 0 when it passes. alarm: in words, when it fails. The value itself does not change. It changes ScanRuler's state in the document.

That zone holds the feature. detail says how many degrees the feature stands off the basic. Other types keep the angle and ignore it. The answer holds the dimension. It changes ScanRuler's state in the document.

report_get.description: Read the measurement report: everything measured on the scan, in one answer. Inputs: format json (default) or text. workspace: measure (the only one here). json: report with what the numbers rest on (units, scale, alignment, fit method, outlier cut-offs). json also holds every element with its fit, and every dimension with value, unit, limit and verdict. It holds checks { checked, pass, fail }; dimensions with no limit are not counted. text: the plain-text summary that ScanRuler's Copy report gives. Per element: its point, direction, size, sigma, used points and form error. Per dimension: its value and verdict. It works with no scan open (an empty report). The answer grows with the count of elements; text is the shorter. Coordinates are in the frame that the scan is measured in now. Changes nothing.

export_csv.description: Write the elements and dimensions as a CSV table, one row each. The columns: [section, id, name, kind, label, value, unit, nominal, plus, minus, max, deviation, verdict, sigma, formError, x, y, z]. section is element or dimension; verdict is PASS or FAIL. x, y, z are mm, in the frame that the scan is measured in now. Input: path: a relative name goes in the folder of the session. Left out, path is <scan>-measurements.csv there. The folder must exist; else it is refused. A file of that name is written over. The answer holds: path and rows. It needs a scan open. Changes nothing in the document.

section_cut.description: Cut the scan with a plane, and keep the cut as a section (shown on ScanRuler's 2D sheet). Inputs: across (needed): an element by id or name, a named plane, an axis with an angle, or a plane. A plane element cuts along itself. A cylinder, cone, line or circle cuts square to its axis, through its centre. "XY", "YZ" or "XZ" cut through the centre of the part. { axis, angleDeg }: a plane that holds an axis ("X", "Y", "Z" or an element with one), turned angleDeg about it. That gives the half section of a turned part. { origin, normal }: a plane. offset slides the plane along its normal, mm. For "XY", "YZ", "XZ", offset is the coordinate itself: "XY" with offset 10 cuts at z = 10. name. kind "shadow" is not a cut: it is the whole scan seen along the normal of the plane. The shadow is its outer boundary: holes are filled, never inside the part. play: mm more round it (negative: a press fit). tolerance: the shadow is read to tolerance mm (0.1). The shadow is the outline for a foam cutout, a bin insert or a holder. Gotchas: a section keeps its points as cut. After the part is moved (align_*, scan_scale, deviation_align), cut again. Sections belong to the scan, and they go when another scan is opened. A closed part gives closed chains, and a scan with holes gives open ones; section_to_sketch leaves those out. The offset of the shadow is made with FreeCAD's 2D offset. It is refused when play is larger than the outline allows. The answer holds: section { id, name, across, offset, plane { origin, normal, basisU, basisV }, chains (how many loops) }. For a shadow, it also holds shadow { play, tolerance, cell, areas } and note. Refused: the plane misses the scan. 0.03 s at 137,000 triangles for a cut (plain Python off the Mac). A shadow rasterises the whole scan and is not measured. Next: section_get (the points), section_fit (lines and arcs), section_to_sketch. It keeps the section in ScanRuler's state; the model is not changed.

oneOf.description: { axis, angleDeg }: a plane through an axis ("X", "Y", "Z" or an element); or { origin, normal }: a plane given outright.

section_get.description: Get the cut of a section as polylines. Inputs: section (needed: id or name). chains: which, by index from 0 (all by default). space: sheet (default), world ([x, y, z]) or both. sheet: [u, v] mm on the sheet of the section, from the origin of the plane along basisU and basisV. limit: 4000 points over all chains; 50000 at most. The answer holds: section, plane { origin, normal, basisU, basisV }, step, and chains. chains: index, closed, points (as cut), kept, length mm, bounds, and sheet and / or world. sheet and world are the points in order; a closed chain ends on its first point. Gotcha: past limit, every k-th point is kept, and step says k. The lengths and bounds are still of every point. To get shapes, not points, use section_fit: it answers lines and arcs in far fewer tokens. Changes nothing.

section_fit.description: Cut the chains of a section into the lines and arcs that they are, without making a sketch. Inputs: section (needed). chains: by index. Or the filters: minLength, maxLength (mm), closedOnly and maxChains. maxChains (12): the longest are kept; leftOut says what the filters dropped. tolerance: mm; by default from the own scatter and point spacing of each chain. detail: 0 to 1 (0.5); higher follows smaller features. arcs: n fits each chain as n arcs end to end. brief: true answers each piece short (id, kind, radius, world ends, rms). The answer holds: section, plane, bounds, sketch, leftOut, and chains. sketch: how a sketch made on this section counts. Its [u, v] is the sheet's plus sketch.add, or a frame of its own. chains: index, closed, points, scatter, scatterFloor, spacing, tolerance and pieces. scatter: mm, the own noise of the chain, as measured off its second differences; 0 on an exact cut. scatterFloor: only where the measured scatter is under it. scatterFloor is 5 % of the point spacing: the least that the fits take the noise of a chain as. So an exact chain still has a noise to weigh a circle against. spacing: mm between points, the median. tolerance: mm, as given, else the larger of three scatters and 0.6 of the spacing. pieces, in order: a line, by a, b, length, angleDeg (from +u, 0 to 180), leanDeg (off the nearest axis). An arc: by center, radius, diameter, start and sweep (radians, counter-clockwise from +u), sweepDeg, a, b. Each piece has points, residual { rms, max } and world coordinates. A chain that will not fit answers error in its row. Gotchas: [u, v] are the sheet of the section, from the origin of the plane, not world coordinates. For "XY", that origin is the centre of the part. Use the world fields to place things. A full circle comes back as one arc whose a and b coincide. On a CAD tessellation, cut after mesh_densify. Else a straight side has only its two end points, and it fits nothing. Size: every point of every chosen chain is fitted. It is declared heavy, so on its own it runs as a job. 0.07 s for 400 points (plain Python off the Mac). A section with tens of thousands of points is not measured. Changes nothing.

arcs.description: Each chain as this many arcs end to end.

chains.description: Which chains, whatever the filters say.

section.description: The section, by id or name.

section_to_sketch.description: Make the last step of the profile road: a FreeCAD Sketcher sketch from a section. The chains of a section are fitted into lines and arcs (as section_fit). They are written as a sketch in a PartDesign Body, on the plane of the section. Inputs: section (needed). body: an existing PartDesign Body, by label or name; left out, a new Body is made. name: the label of the sketch ("<section> sketch" by default). chains, minLength, maxLength, maxChains, tolerance, detail and arcs: as section_fit. closedOnly: true by default; only closed chains, unless chains names them. What it makes: one Sketcher::SketchObject, not attached (Map Mode Deactivated). Its Placement is on the plane of the section. Zero is at the foot of the world origin on the plane. x is along the coordinate axis next round. It holds lines, arcs of circle and full circles. Neighbouring pieces meet where their carriers cross, and Coincident constraints join them. No dimensions or other constraints are added: the sketch is under-constrained, as traced. Gotchas: the Placement is written inside the own coordinates of the Body. So a Body that has been moved puts the sketch off the scan: use a Body at the origin. The sketch does not follow the section or the scan afterwards. An open chain gives an open wire, which a pad will refuse. Where two neighbouring pieces do not meet, a short bridging line joins them (bridges counts them). The answer holds: sketch and body (labels), section, frame { origin, xAxis, yAxis, normal }, fitted, wires, leftOut, and health from the shared check. fitted, per chain: { index, closed, lines, arcs, circles, bridges, tolerance, scatter, scatterFloor }, or error. scatter: the noise of the chain as measured, 0 on an exact cut. scatterFloor: as section_fit, only where the measured scatter is under it. wires [{ closed, edges }]: as FreeCAD built them after a recompute; check that every wire is closed. Then pd_pad: next gives the call with the labels that came out. A new Body takes the next free label of FreeCAD ("Body002" where objects named Body and Body001 exist). So read the body of the answer, and never assume "Body". Or make the Body first (pd_body_new { name }), and give it as body. Refused: the section has no closed chain (give chains, or closedOnly: false). One undo step.

arcs.description: Each chain as this many arcs end to end.

chains.description: Which chains, whatever the filters say.

section.description: The section, by id or name.

section_to_sketch.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/sections.py

mesh_parts.description: Read what Mesh Tools holds beside the scan. Read it before and after edits. It needs a scan open (scan_open). The answer holds: scan { name, triangles, edits (those taken into use) }, and edited { triangles, edits (pending) } or null. It holds reduced (the report of mesh_reduce) or null. It holds wrap { triangles } and piece { name, triangles }, or null: the previews that mesh_wrap and mesh_trim leave. It holds undo: the step that mesh_undo would take back, or null. None of these is a FreeCAD document object. object_list does not show them, and FreeCAD's undo does not touch them. mesh_export { to: "document" } puts one in the document. Changes nothing.
mesh_parts.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_inspect.description: Find what the tools would find on the mesh worked on. That is the edited copy, or the scan while there is none. The answer holds: working, vertices, triangles, bounds { min, max }, open, bad, volume, islands and holes. open: open edges; 0 = closed. bad: edges that more than two triangles share. volume: mm³, only when closed, else null; negative = inside out (mesh_flip_normals). islands { size, pieces (connected pieces), islands (those smaller than size), islandTriangles, largestIsland, smallestKept, centres }. holes { size, rims (open rims in all), holes (those smaller than size), largestHole, smallestOpen, centres }. centres are [x, y, z] mm, the first 40. The centre of a hole is what mesh_fill_holes { at } takes. The size of a piece is the diagonal of its bounding box. The size of a hole is the widest span of its rim. pieceSize defaults to a hundredth of the diagonal of the part, and holeSize to a twentieth. Both are rounded to 1-2-5 steps, and the answer says them. Run it before and after each edit. It reads every triangle: about 2 s at 130,000 triangles and 13 s at 520,000. That is where this pass timed it: a Linux container, not the Mac. Past 45 s, it answers as a job (job_status { job }). Changes nothing.
mesh_inspect.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_remove_islands.description: Delete every connected piece smaller across than size, mm (the diagonal of its bounding box). These are specks, or a patch of turntable; every larger piece stays. size defaults to a hundredth of the diagonal of the part (1-2-5 rounded). Refused: no piece is that small; the message gives the smallest piece. Refused: all pieces are that small, so nothing would be left. mesh_inspect { pieceSize } counts them first. It works on the edited copy; the first edit makes it from the scan. The measuring tools keep reading the scan until mesh_use_edited. It is not a FreeCAD document change: mesh_undo takes it back (20 steps), and FreeCAD's undo does not. The answer holds: edit, report { pieces, islands, islandTriangles, largestIsland, smallestKept }, and mesh { working ("scan" or "edited copy"), vertices, triangles, bounds, open (open edges), bad (edges more than two triangles share), volume (mm³; null unless closed; negative when inside out), edits }.
mesh_remove_islands.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_delete_marked.description: Delete the surface that a region holds. A triangle goes when all three of its corners are in the region. The hole that it leaves stays open (mesh_fill_holes closes it). region: exactly one of { box: { min: [x, y, z], max } }, { sphere: { center, radius } } or { vertices: [n, …] }. The values are mm, in the frame that the scan is in now. facing: [x, y, z] and angleDeg (30) narrow it to the vertices whose normal points that way. "marked" (the marking of the person on screen) is refused here: FreeCAD has no such marking. Trap: vertex numbers read on the scan (scan_query, scan_segment) can go stale. They are refused once the vertices of the edited copy are numbered differently. Then use a box or a sphere. Refused: no triangle lies wholly inside, or all do. It works on the edited copy; the first edit makes it from the scan. The measuring tools keep reading the scan until mesh_use_edited. It is not a FreeCAD document change: mesh_undo takes it back (20 steps), and FreeCAD's undo does not. The answer holds: edit, report { triangles (deleted) }, and mesh { working ("scan" or "edited copy"), vertices, triangles, bounds, open (open edges), bad (edges more than two triangles share), volume (mm³; null unless closed; negative when inside out), edits }. Afterwards, open is above 0 and volume is null.

oneOf.description: Exactly one of box { min, max }, sphere { center, radius } or vertices [..], narrowed with facing [x, y, z] and angleDeg (30 to start).

mesh_delete_marked.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_flip_normals.description: Turn triangles over: every one, or those with all three corners in region. region: as mesh_delete_marked takes it (box, sphere or vertices, with facing). Use it for a part exported inside out (mesh_inspect shows a negative volume), or for patches that face inwards. Flipping a correct closed mesh makes its volume negative; flipping again restores it. It works on the edited copy; the first edit makes it from the scan. The measuring tools keep reading the scan until mesh_use_edited. It is not a FreeCAD document change: mesh_undo takes it back (20 steps), and FreeCAD's undo does not. The answer holds: edit, report { triangles (turned) }, and mesh { working ("scan" or "edited copy"), vertices, triangles, bounds, open (open edges), bad (edges more than two triangles share), volume (mm³; null unless closed; negative when inside out), edits }.

oneOf.description: Exactly one of box { min, max }, sphere { center, radius } or vertices [..], narrowed with facing [x, y, z] and angleDeg (30 to start).

mesh_cut.description: Cut the mesh with a plane, and take one side off. plane: "XY", "YZ" or "XZ", or an element with a direction, by id or name. For "XY", "YZ" or "XZ", offset is the coordinate of the plane. That is Z for XY, X for YZ, Y for XZ. The element is a plane, cylinder, cone, line or circle from element_list. For an element, offset slides along its direction from its own position. keep: plus keeps the side that the direction points to (above XY, +X of YZ, +Y of XZ). keep: minus keeps the other side. cap (true by default) closes the part flat wherever the plane goes all the way round the cut. cap bridges short gaps of a hole right at the cut. Where it cannot, the cut stays open (report.open). Refused: the plane leaves everything on one side; the message gives the offsets that the mesh runs between. mesh_cut_preview tries a place without cutting. It works on the edited copy; the first edit makes it from the scan. The measuring tools keep reading the scan until mesh_use_edited. It is not a FreeCAD document change: mesh_undo takes it back (20 steps), and FreeCAD's undo does not. The answer holds: edit, report { removed, split (triangles), capped (faces closed), capTriangles, open (stretches left open), bridged }, and mesh { working ("scan" or "edited copy"), vertices, triangles, bounds, open (open edges), bad (edges more than two triangles share), volume (mm³; null unless closed; negative when inside out), edits }. It clips every triangle that the plane crosses, in Python. About 5 s at 130,000 triangles and 16 s at 520,000, where this pass timed it. That was a Linux container, not the Mac. Past 45 s, it answers as a job.

keep.description: plus: the side the plane's direction points to (above XY, +X of YZ, +Y of XZ, along an element's direction); minus the other.

offset.description: mm: a coordinate plane's coordinate, or along an element's direction.

plane.description: A coordinate plane — "XY", "YZ" or "XZ" — or an element with a direction, by id or name.

mesh_cut.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_cut_preview.description: Find what mesh_cut at this plane would do, without cutting. plane, offset and keep: as mesh_cut takes them (keep plus by default). The answer holds: plane (its words), cuts, capped, bridged, open. cuts: false when everything lies on one side; then the rest are 0. capped: faces that a cap would close. bridged: gaps bridged. open: stretches that a cap would leave open. It costs about what the cut does: it clips the mesh and throws the result away. Past 45 s, it answers as a job. Changes nothing.

keep.description: plus: the side the plane's direction points to (above XY, +X of YZ, +Y of XZ, along an element's direction); minus the other.

plane.description: A coordinate plane — "XY", "YZ" or "XZ" — or an element with a direction, by id or name.

mesh_cut_preview.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_mirror.description: Reflect the mesh across a plane. plane and offset: as mesh_cut takes them. Left out, offset goes through the middle of the bounding box of the mesh worked on. That middle is rounded to a 1-2-5 step of about a fiftieth of its diagonal. So it is not always the exact middle. The text of the edit says where. An offset given is taken as it is. mode whole (the default) reflects all of it: the part moves to the other side, mirrored. mode symmetric keeps the side that keep names (plus by default), and replaces the other with its reflection. The two are joined along the plane, so a closed part stays closed. Use it to rebuild a damaged side from the good one. Refused: nothing lies on the side to keep. It works on the edited copy; the first edit makes it from the scan. The measuring tools keep reading the scan until mesh_use_edited. It is not a FreeCAD document change: mesh_undo takes it back (20 steps), and FreeCAD's undo does not. The answer holds: edit (its text says the plane used), report { mode, mirrored, removed, split, inPlane (triangles) }, and mesh { working ("scan" or "edited copy"), vertices, triangles, bounds, open (open edges), bad (edges more than two triangles share), volume (mm³; null unless closed; negative when inside out), edits }.

keep.description: plus: the side the plane's direction points to (above XY, +X of YZ, +Y of XZ, along an element's direction); minus the other.

plane.description: A coordinate plane — "XY", "YZ" or "XZ" — or an element with a direction, by id or name.

mesh_mirror.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_fill_holes.description: Close the holes (open rims) smaller across than size, mm. size: a twentieth of the diagonal of the part by default, 1-2-5 rounded. With at: [x, y, z], it closes only the one of those holes whose middle is nearest that point. at does not lift the size limit: pass a size above the size of the hole too. mesh_inspect { holeSize } gives the middle of each hole and the sizes. patch: curved (the default) continues the bending of the surface across the hole. patch: flat lays the tightest patch. Each patch is triangulated to bend least (Liepa), refined to the density round it, and faired. The own vertices of the mesh do not move. Trap: an opening that the part really has (a bore, a slot seen as a rim) is closed too. So fill by at. Refused, with the size of the smallest rim: no rim is under size. Refused: the mesh has no open rim. It works on the edited copy; the first edit makes it from the scan. The measuring tools keep reading the scan until mesh_use_edited. It is not a FreeCAD document change: mesh_undo takes it back (20 steps), and FreeCAD's undo does not. The answer holds: edit, report { filled, triangles, vertices (added), failed (rims that could not be patched), left (rims over size) }, and mesh { working ("scan" or "edited copy"), vertices, triangles, bounds, open (open edges), bad (edges more than two triangles share), volume (mm³; null unless closed; negative when inside out), edits }. The mesh is closed when open is 0.
mesh_fill_holes.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_smooth.description: Smooth the scatter of a scan out. Each point is moved along its normal onto a quadric fitted to the mesh round it. The quadric is fitted over a patch size across (mm). Bumps smaller than size go; shape larger than it stays. No point moves further than limit, mm. size defaults to the larger of 0.8 % of the diagonal of the part and 2.5 mean edge lengths. limit defaults to a thousandth of the diagonal. Both are 1-2-5 rounded; the settings of the answer say both. keepEdges (true by default) fits each side of an edge sharper than 30° alone, and leaves the edge as scanned. region (as mesh_delete_marked takes it) moves only that surface, fading to its edge. Trap: a large size rounds real edges and small features off. Keep limit near the noise of the scan (scan_qa reads it). A CAD-exact mesh has nothing to smooth: points move by rounding only. It works on the edited copy; the first edit makes it from the scan. The measuring tools keep reading the scan until mesh_use_edited. It is not a FreeCAD document change: mesh_undo takes it back (20 steps), and FreeCAD's undo does not. The answer holds: edit, report { settings, region, moved, held (points kept on an edge), maxMove, rmsMove (mm), atLimit }, and mesh { working ("scan" or "edited copy"), vertices, triangles, bounds, open (open edges), bad (edges more than two triangles share), volume (mm³; null unless closed; negative when inside out), edits }. It is the slowest edit: it fits a patch per vertex in Python. About 40 s at 130,000 triangles, where this pass timed it (a Linux container, not the Mac). So it takes several minutes at a million. Past 45 s, it answers as a job (job_status). On a large scan, use mesh_reduce first, or give a region.

oneOf.description: Exactly one of box { min, max }, sphere { center, radius } or vertices [..], narrowed with facing [x, y, z] and angleDeg (30 to start).

mesh_smooth.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_offset.description: Move the whole surface along its normal by distance, mm. direction: expand (the part grows) or shrink. It is not a scale: every face ends the distance from where it was, and edges stay sharp. For example, a box 40 × 30 × 20 expanded by 1 is 42 × 32 × 22. A corner point moves up to √3 times the distance, never more than 3 times. region is refused (moving only a marked region is not ported): leave it out. Trap: shrinking by more than half the thickness of a wall turns that wall inside out. Nothing checks it: look at the volume and view_render afterwards. It works on the edited copy; the first edit makes it from the scan. The measuring tools keep reading the scan until mesh_use_edited. It is not a FreeCAD document change: mesh_undo takes it back (20 steps), and FreeCAD's undo does not. The answer holds: edit, report { distance (signed), moved, maxMove }, and mesh { working ("scan" or "edited copy"), vertices, triangles, bounds, open (open edges), bad (edges more than two triangles share), volume (mm³; null unless closed; negative when inside out), edits }. About 1.5 s at 130,000 triangles and 10 s at 520,000, where this pass timed it. That was a Linux container, not the Mac. Past 45 s, it answers as a job.

oneOf.description: Exactly one of box { min, max }, sphere { center, radius } or vertices [..], narrowed with facing [x, y, z] and angleDeg (30 to start).

mesh_offset.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_reduce.description: Make a light mesh for CAD from the mesh worked on, by FreeCAD's quadric decimation (Mesh.decimate(targetSize)). Its other form, decimate(tolerance, reduction), holds no tolerance in millimetres either, and it is not used. The result is the lightest mesh that still lies within tolerance of the original, measured both ways. tolerance: mm; a quarter of a thousandth of the diagonal of the part by default, 1-2-5 rounded. The tolerance is held in millimetres; FreeCAD's decimator has no such bound of its own. Asked for a count, the decimator gives the best mesh of that size, whatever it costs in shape. So the count is searched: each try is decimated and measured. The search takes off a quarter of the triangles at a time. It goes on while 99.9 % of the sampled points lie within tolerance both ways. Then it searches between the last count that held and the first that did not. tries says how many decimations; about a dozen. maxTriangles (50,000) is the harder rule: a mesh with more is brought down to it first. When that mesh does not hold the tolerance, the answer says so: capped: true, held: false, won: "cap". A warning then says how far off it lies. That mesh is not one to measure or model on: raise maxTriangles or the tolerance. The search then goes on above the cap, for the smallest count that does hold the tolerance. It halves the gap between a count that does not hold and one that does. It makes 8 tries at most, and the whole search takes 30 s at most. holds { asked, triangles, passes, p999, max, backP999, backMax } is the row of that mesh. The warning names its count as the maxTriangles to ask for. notHolding is the largest count tried that did not hold, so the true count lies between the two. With no holds, the warning says that none was found, and in how many tries. The cap is kept exactly, or the answer says that it is not. FreeCAD's decimator can stop above the count asked. It makes a hundred rounds at most, and never a collapse that would turn a triangle over. Asking it for less changes nothing, so it is run again on what it left. passes: at most 6 runs, until one takes nothing off. Even that can stay above the cap: then capMet: false, won: "tolerance", and the cap cannot win. atCap { asked, triangles, passes, p999, max, backP999, backMax } is what the decimator left there (the true count, and how far off). The answer is then the lightest mesh found that holds the tolerance (over the cap: triangles says how many). Or it is that try itself, when it holds, or the mesh as it is. The warning says which, with the counts. won is "both" when the cap and the tolerance both hold. The search then goes on down from the cap, for the lightest. won is null when the mesh was under the cap to begin with. Every count and distance in the warning is a figure of the answer. When no lighter mesh holds the tolerance, the answer is the mesh as it is, with a note. It is a preview beside the mesh, not an edit. mesh_apply_reduced makes it the edited copy. mesh_export { part: "reduced" } writes it. mesh_discard { what: "reduced" } drops it. A second mesh_reduce replaces it. The answer holds: reduced { settings, inputTriangles, triangles, vertices, measured, within, p999, max, rms, backP999, backMax, held, capped, capMet, won, tries, search, atCap, holds, notHolding, method, note | warning }. measured: points sampled, at most 4000. rms: original to reduced, mm. backP999, backMax: reduced to original, read at the vertices of the reduced mesh and at the middles of its triangles. A triangle that cuts a corner off has its vertices on the original. held: 99.9 % within tolerance both ways. capped: the cap came first, and the tolerance does not hold. capMet: triangles is at most maxTriangles. search { tries, ms, ended, seconds }: ended is "done", or "time" when the 30 s ran out. What was found by then is kept. atCap, holds and notHolding come only when they apply. Cost: one FreeCAD decimation for each try, more when it stops above the count (passes). Each try also has two distance checks of 4,000 points. There are a dozen tries or so, and up to 8 more when the cap does not hold the tolerance. The checks take about half a second a try at 220,000 triangles in a Linux container. FreeCAD's own decimation comes on top; it is not measured on the Mac. Past 45 s, it answers as a job.
mesh_reduce.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_apply_reduced.description: Make the reduced mesh that mesh_reduce left into the edited copy. It is one undo step: mesh_undo puts back the mesh that it was made of. The reduced preview is then gone. Refused: there is none (mesh_reduce makes one; mesh_parts says). A reduction that did not hold its tolerance (held: false: the cap came first) is applied all the same. A warning then says how far off it lies, and where mesh_reduce found it, the count that would hold. mesh_undo takes it back. One over the cap asked is applied too (capMet: false: FreeCAD's decimator stopped above it). A warning then gives its count, the cap, and where the decimator stopped. Every vertex number changes. It is not a FreeCAD document change. The answer holds: edit, report (the reduction's), warning, and mesh { working ("scan" or "edited copy"), vertices, triangles, bounds, open (open edges), bad (edges more than two triangles share), volume (mm³; null unless closed; negative when inside out), edits }. warning comes when it did not hold its tolerance, or is over its cap.
mesh_apply_reduced.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_discard.description: Throw a preview away without applying it. what: "reduced" (the light mesh of mesh_reduce) or "wrap" (the skin of mesh_wrap). Refused: there is none of that kind (mesh_parts says what is on hand). The mesh worked on is not touched; no undo step. The answer holds: discarded.
mesh_discard.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_use_edited.description: Take the edited copy into use. It becomes the scan that every tool measures (scan_info, element_fit, sections, deviation, thickness). The sections kept are cut again on it. Elements fitted before keep their old fits, and vertex numbers read before no longer match. So fit again where it matters. From then on, the scan shown in the FreeCAD document is the edited mesh. Its mesh object is put in again. Refused: there is no edited copy. One mesh_undo goes back to the scan before; FreeCAD's undo does not. The answer holds: scan { name, triangles, edits (all taken into use so far) }, note.
mesh_use_edited.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_discard_edited.description: Throw the edited copy and its pending edits away: the tools work on the scan in use again. Refused: there is no edited copy. One mesh_undo brings the copy back. Previews (reduced, wrap, piece) stay. The answer holds: mesh { working ("scan" or "edited copy"), vertices, triangles, bounds, open (open edges), bad (edges more than two triangles share), volume (mm³; null unless closed; negative when inside out), edits }.
mesh_discard_edited.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_undo.description: Take the last Mesh Tools step back: an edit, mesh_use_edited, mesh_discard_edited, mesh_apply_reduced or mesh_apply_wrap. The arrays before each step are kept, 20 steps deep; there is no redo. This is the own undo of Mesh Tools. FreeCAD's undo (history_undo) does not take a mesh edit back. mesh_undo does not undo a document change: a mesh_export to the document stays. Undoing mesh_use_edited cuts the sections again on the scan before. Refused: there is nothing to take back (mesh_parts: undo null). The answer holds: undone (the label of the step), and mesh { working ("scan" or "edited copy"), vertices, triangles, bounds, open (open edges), bad (edges more than two triangles share), volume (mm³; null unless closed; negative when inside out), edits }.
mesh_undo.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_export.description: Write one of the meshes of Mesh Tools out. part: edited (the edited copy), reduced (of mesh_reduce), piece (of mesh_trim) or wrap (the preview of mesh_wrap). A part that does not exist is refused (mesh_parts says). The scan itself is not a part: a mesh edit first makes a copy. to file (the default): a binary STL in millimetres, or format 3mf, at path. path: relative means the folder of the session; the extension of the format is added when missing. The default path is <scan name>-<part>.<format> there. The answer then holds: file { path, name, bytes }, format, triangles. to document: a Mesh::Feature labelled "<scan name> <part>" in the FreeCAD document. There the meshobj tools, slicing and export work on it, and scan_open { object } takes it back in. That is one FreeCAD undo step; the answer holds: object (its label), triangles, health. It is a copy as it is now: later mesh edits do not follow into the file or the object. It builds FreeCAD's mesh triangle by triangle in Python. About 5 s at 520,000 triangles, where this pass timed it (a Linux container, not the Mac). The write comes on top.
mesh_export.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/meshtools.py

mesh_densify.description: Cut the triangles until no edge is longer than maxEdge, mm, with the surface unchanged. Every new vertex is the middle of an edge, on the facet that it was cut from. The mesh stays as closed as it was (volume the same). Use it for a mesh exported from CAD, whose vertices lie only on its edges and rims. For example, a box is 8 vertices, 12 triangles. Only after it do these find points inside its faces: the vertex method of scan_segment, a seeded element_fit, section_fit, mesh_smooth and mesh_trim. A real scan needs none. maxEdge defaults to a hundredth of the diagonal of the part, on the 1-2-5 steps. Each halving of maxEdge is four times the triangles (the 40 × 30 × 20 box at maxEdge 2: 8,192). A result past 20 million is refused. It works on the edited copy; the first edit makes it from the scan. The measuring tools keep reading the scan until mesh_use_edited. It is not a FreeCAD document change: mesh_undo takes it back (20 steps), and FreeCAD's undo does not. The answer holds: edit { maxEdge, trianglesBefore, triangles, added (vertices), longest (edge now), passes }, status, and mesh { working ("scan" or "edited copy"), vertices, triangles, bounds, open (open edges), bad (edges more than two triangles share), volume (mm³; null unless closed; negative when inside out), edits }. It is vectorised: under a second to half a million triangles, where this pass timed it. That was a Linux container, not the Mac.

maxEdge.description: No edge longer than this, mm.

mesh_densify.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/meshtools/handlers.py

mesh_boolean.description: Make the mesh and solids one. op: subtract (take them out of it), add (join them to it) or intersect (keep what both hold). solids: measured cylinders, cones and spheres, or solid bodies in the FreeCAD document. An element is given by id or name, and drawn at its assumed diameter when one is set. A body is given by Name or Label. It is a shape with a solid, tessellated to 0.01 mm, or a closed mesh object. An App::Part round it is followed. Several solids go as one: their union. The mesh worked on must be closed (mesh_inspect: open 0; mesh_fill_holes first), and so must each solid. Refused, naming the solid: a solid taken away that does not reach the mesh. Refused: a solid taken away that lies wholly inside the mesh. It would seal a hollow: carry its end out through the surface. Refused: a solid added that lies wholly inside. A solid that only grazes the mesh can fail to come out closed: move it a little. For a bore that the scanner could not see to the bottom of, fit a cylinder to its wall. Make it longer than the bore and out through the surface, and subtract it. A document body is read as it stands now: later changes to it do not follow. Dense scans are cut as they are: every triangle that the solids do not touch is kept. It works on the edited copy; the first edit makes it from the scan. The measuring tools keep reading the scan until mesh_use_edited. It is not a FreeCAD document change: mesh_undo takes it back (20 steps), and FreeCAD's undo does not. The answer holds: edit { op, removed, added (triangles), volumeBefore, volumeAfter, solid, volume (the change, mm³) }, status, and mesh { working ("scan" or "edited copy"), vertices, triangles, bounds, open (open edges), bad (edges more than two triangles share), volume (mm³; null unless closed; negative when inside out), edits }. About 2 s on 130,000 triangles with a 400-triangle cylinder, where this pass timed it. That was a Linux container, not the Mac; it is not declared heavy.

solids.description: The solids, by element id or name, or document object Name or Label.

mesh_boolean.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/meshtools/handlers.py
