mesh_shell.description: Hollow a closed part, or thicken an open surface. mode: left out, it picks by the mesh. hollow (closed mesh): the outside stays as it is. An inner wall thickness mm in from it seals a cavity. Where the part is thinner than twice the wall, it stays solid. Refused: the part is nowhere thicker than that. The inner wall is built on a grid, and it comes out dense. The grid cell is in the answer: about a third of the thickness. For example, the 40 × 30 × 20 box at thickness 2 gets 68,000 triangles. It loses 14,951 mm³ against the exact 14,976. The cavity is sealed: no drain hole is made (mesh_boolean subtract opens one). thicken (open mesh: one side of a part, a sheet): a second skin thickness from it. side: in (the default: the scanned surface stays the outside), out or both. A wall goes round every rim. A part closed but for holes smaller than the default size of mesh_fill_holes is refused, unless told which. Fill the holes to hollow it, or pass mode: "thicken". mode hollow on an open mesh is refused, and so is thicken on a closed one. thickness defaults to a 125th of the diagonal of the part. It works on the edited copy; the first edit makes it from the scan. The measuring tools keep reading the scan until mesh_use_edited. It is not a FreeCAD document change: mesh_undo takes it back (20 steps), and FreeCAD's undo does not. The answer holds: edit { mode, thickness, cell, cavities, removed (mm³), volumeBefore, triangles (of the new wall) }, status, and mesh { working ("scan" or "edited copy"), vertices, triangles, bounds, open (open edges), bad (edges more than two triangles share), volume (mm³; null unless closed; negative when inside out), edits }. Heavy: the grid work is bounded at 12 million points. 1 to 5 s on the box up to 86,000 triangles, where this pass timed it. That was a Linux container, not the Mac. Larger is not measured. Past 45 s, it answers as a job.

thickness.description: The wall a hollow leaves, or the thickness a surface is given, mm.

side.description: For a surface: which way the wall grows from it — in to start.

mode.description: What to do; absent, what the mesh calls for.

mesh_shell.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/meshtools/handlers.py

mesh_wrap.description: Make one closed skin round the mesh worked on, for a mesh that is a mess inside. Examples: an assembly exported as one file, channels inside a casting, overlapping or flipped shells, a scan with cracks. Any triangles do: only the distance to them is used. A ball of diameter gap (mm) is rolled round the mesh from outside. The wrap lies on the part where the ball touched it, and it bridges every opening narrower than gap. A groove narrower than gap is closed over too, so keep gap small. Everything inside is dropped. grow (0 by default, at most gap) stands the wrap off the part all round. At 0, an open sheet wraps to nothing (refused, saying so). With grow, it wraps to a slab 2 × grow thick. edges: sharp (the default) rebuilds the sharp edges and corners of the part where the wrap lies on the part. edges: smooth leaves them rounded by the grid, a sixth of the gap. tolerance is accepted and not used yet (no reducer is ported). So the wrap comes out dense (the 40 × 30 × 20 box at gap 4: 25,548 triangles). Use mesh_apply_wrap, then mesh_reduce. It is made beside the mesh as a preview. mesh_apply_wrap makes it the edited copy. mesh_export { part: "wrap" } writes it. mesh_discard { what: "wrap" } drops it. preview: false applies it at once; the answer then also holds the edit and mesh. The answer holds: wrap { settings, shells, triangles, vertices, area, dropped, bridgedArea (mm²), volumeBefore, volume (mm³), cell (the grid, mm), coarsened, fullGap, gridPoints, sharpEdges, sharpCorners, from }, status. dropped: input triangles inside it. volumeBefore: null when the mesh is open. coarsened and fullGap: when the size of the part made the grid coarser than a sixth of the gap. A gap too fine for the part is refused, with the smallest gap that works. Heavy: the cost grows with the triangles of the input, and with the grid. The grid has at most 6 million grid points. 2 s for the 12-triangle box, but 6 minutes for an 86,000-triangle mesh at the same gap. That is where this pass timed it: a Linux container, not the Mac. It runs as a job: past 45 s it answers with a job id (job_status { job, wait }). On a dense mesh, use mesh_reduce and mesh_apply_reduced first.

gap.description: Openings narrower than this are bridged, mm.

grow.description: How far the wrap stands off the part, mm: 0 to start, at most gap.

tolerance.description: How far the wrap's reduction may stray from it, mm (kept for when a reducer is ported).

preview.description: false applies the wrap at once as the edited copy; true (to start) leaves it a preview for mesh_apply_wrap.

mesh_wrap.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/meshtools/handlers.py

mesh_apply_wrap.description: Make the wrap that mesh_wrap left into the edited copy. The tools work on it from here, and mesh_use_edited takes it into use for measuring. None of the own vertices of the mesh is kept: every vertex number changes. It is one undo step (mesh_undo), which puts back the mesh that it was made of. The wrap preview is gone either way. Refused: there is no wrap (mesh_parts says). It is not a FreeCAD document change. The answer holds: edit { triangles }, status, and mesh { working ("scan" or "edited copy"), vertices, triangles, bounds, open (open edges), bad (edges more than two triangles share), volume (mm³; null unless closed; negative when inside out), edits }.
mesh_apply_wrap.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/meshtools/handlers.py

mesh_trim.description: Mend a broken part: cut a body with the scanned fracture, to print and glue in. The body is the missing piece, modelled to the nominal shape of the part, standing where it belongs. It is a few millimetres too long at the break. body: a solid body in the FreeCAD document (Name or Label; read as it stands now). Or body is a measured cylinder, cone or sphere (element id or name). The break is found where the mesh worked on lies deeper inside the body than depth (0.3 mm by default). region marks the break instead: { box }, { sphere } or { vertices }, optionally with facing, as mesh_delete_marked takes it. offset sets the mating face back from the break, mm. offset 0 cuts on the break; 0.1 to 0.2 leaves room for glue. flip: true keeps what is on the other side of the break. The break is read at the vertices of the mesh. On a CAD-style mesh with vertices only on its edges, it finds nothing until mesh_densify; the refusal says so. Refusals say which step failed. That is: the body does not reach into the part. Or: the break does not come out of the body (mark it wider). Or: nothing is on that side (flip). The piece is made beside the mesh: it is not an edit of the mesh, and not a document object. mesh_export { part: "piece" } writes it (to: "document" for a mesh object). A second mesh_trim replaces it. The answer holds: piece { name, solid, triangles, volume (mm³), matingArea (mm²), bodyVolume, offset, pieces, dropped (pieces on the other side), break { depth, triangles, area }, fit }, status. fit { min, median, max … }: how far the mating face is from the part, mm. Example: a 10 mm cube reaching 5 mm into a densified block gives volume 499 of 1000 and matingArea 100. Heavy: it runs as a job past 45 s. Under a second to 130,000 triangles, where this pass timed it (a Linux container, not the Mac). The surface search can refuse a mesh over about 4 million triangles, and it says so. Then use mesh_reduce and mesh_apply_reduced first.

offset.description: How far the mating face sits back from the break, mm.

depth.description: How much deeper in the body than its surface the scan must lie to be break, mm.

flip.description: Keep what is on the other side of the break.

region.description: The surface: { box: { min, max } }, { sphere: { center, radius } } or { vertices: [...] } (as mesh_smooth takes), optionally with facing.

mesh_trim.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/meshtools/handlers.py

flat_objects.description: Find the separate parts on the flatbed image. A grey level parts them from the background: Otsu's, unless threshold 0–255 is given. dark: whether the parts are darker than the background; by default, read from the border of the image. The parts are numbered from 1 in reading order: rows from the top of the sheet down, left to right. flat_profile { object } takes that number. It needs an image on the sheet: refused on a section, and before flat_open_image. The answer holds: units, threshold and dark (as used), count, objects, more, note. objects [{ object, area, holes, box { min, max }, centroid, equivalentDiameter, feret { max, maxAngleDeg, min, minAngleDeg }, axisAngleDeg, outline }]. area: sheet units², holes taken out. equivalentDiameter: of a circle of that area. feret: the largest and smallest caliper widths. axisAngleDeg: the long axis. outline: with outline: true, thinned to a few hundred points. objects holds the first limit (100); more says how many were left out. minArea drops specks (sheet units²; by default 400 pixels' worth). minHoleArea: the holes counted (minArea by default). Uncalibrated, every length is in pixels: check units. The numbers are kept for flat_profile until another image, a section or flat_calibrate replaces them. Worked example: a black disc of radius 8 mm at 10 px/mm reads area 201.08 (π·8² = 201.06). It reads equivalentDiameter 16.00 and feret.min 16.0. About 1 s at 16 megapixels, where this pass timed it (a Linux container, not the Mac). It changes nothing on the elements of the sheet.
flat_objects.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

flat_profile.description: Read an outline against a centre or along an axis, and count its peaks by prominence. kind radial (the default): a part seen from above. For example, the teeth of a knurl or a gear round it. kind axial: a part lying on its side; each side is read apart. The outline: object or chains. object: a number from flat_objects; image only. chains: edge chains by number from flat_edges; the only way on a section. Several chains are joined in the order given. about: a 2D element by id or name: a circle, arc or point for radial, a line for axial. Left out, about is the own centroid or long axis of the object. For chains, it is the mean of their points, and their principal axis. The answer holds: units, about { kind, center | origin, dir }, prominence (as used), and sides. sides: one for radial; two for axial ([0] left of the direction of the axis, [1] right). Each side: { peaks (count), max, min, peakMean, valleyMean, depth (peakMean − valleyMean), pitch, pitchUnit }. pitch and pitchUnit: degrees for radial, sheet units for axial; only with peaks. detail: "full" adds peakList [{ at, position, value, prominence }]. samples (3 to 4096) and prominence override the defaults. The default prominence is never under 1.5 pixels (1.5 mm on a section). So shallow teeth on a section need prominence given. A round disc reads 0 peaks, with max and min both near its radius. Refused: object before flat_objects. Refused: chain numbers that the sheet does not have. Refused: about of the wrong kind. Changes nothing.
flat_profile.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

flat_open_image.description: Open a flatbed scan of a part on the 2D sheet, in place of what was there. Then find its edges. What was there goes: its elements, dimensions, notes, alignment and object numbers. path: a PNG, or a JPEG or other format where the image reader of Qt loads it. A relative path means the folder of the session; the image is read as 8-bit grey. Without Qt, only a PNG that is not interlaced, 8 or 16 bits a channel, is read (slowly, in Python). The scale that the file declares (PNG pHYs, JPEG JFIF density) is taken as millimetres. That holds until flat_calibrate sets a measured one; the report calls it nominal. With none declared, the sheet is in pixels (units "px"), and every length reads in pixels until calibrated. The 2D sheet holds one subject: a flatbed image (flat_open_image), or the section cut last (section_cut puts it there). Places are [x, y] in the units of the sheet. They are millimetres once calibrated (a section always is), pixels before. The zero of an image is its bottom-left corner. The zero of a section is the centre of the cutting plane. +X is right, +Y is up. The answer holds: flat { subject, image { fileName, width, height (pixels), decoder ("QImage" or "png (zlib)") }, units, calibration { source (metadata | none | measured), pxPerMm }, edges { chains, sensitivity }, elements, dimensions }. Size: edge finding holds about ten arrays of 8 bytes a pixel (source: flat_core.detect_edges). That is near 1.3 GB at 16 megapixels. That took 4 s where this pass timed it (a Linux container, not the Mac). A 600 dpi A4 scan is 35 megapixels, 1200 dpi 140. Crop to the part, or scan at a lower resolution, rather than open those whole (not measured on the Mac). Heavy: past 45 s, it answers as a job (job_status). It is session state, not a FreeCAD document change: FreeCAD's undo does not take it back. Every flat_ answer names the sheet that it read or changed (sheet: kind image or section, name, scale). A refusal here says which sheet stays.
flat_open_image.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

flat_calibrate.description: Set the scale of the image against a known length, both axes alike. mode distance: points are exactly two places a known distance apart. mode diameter: three or more places on the edge of a circle of known diameter. mm is that true length. Places are in the units of the sheet as they are now. That is pixels on an uncalibrated image, the nominal millimetres otherwise. Everything on the sheet keeps its place on the image, and is scaled to the new units. That is elements, notes and the alignment. The edges are found again, so chain numbers change. The numbers of flat_objects are dropped: run it again. Refused: on a section (already millimetres). Refused: the wrong number of points. Refused: two points that coincide. The answer holds: calibration { source: "measured", pxPerMm { x, y }, dpi }, chains, units, scaledBy (new place = old place × this), note. Worked example: two points 10 units apart given as mm: 20 doubles every length (scaledBy 2). It costs what finding the edges does (see flat_open_image); heavy. It is session state, not a FreeCAD document change: FreeCAD's undo does not take it back.
flat_calibrate.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

flat_detect_edges.description: Find the edges of the image again at a sensitivity from 0 (only the strongest) to 1 (every faint one). Left out, sensitivity is the one last used (0.5 at first). The edges are subpixel Canny chains, with gaps bridged. Chains under a millimetre (24 pixels when uncalibrated) and texture are dropped. Chain numbers change with every detection: read flat_edges again before you name chains. Elements already fitted stay as they are. On a section it changes nothing: the cut is its edges, and the answer says so. The answer holds: chains (how many), note (on a section). It costs what opening the image did; heavy (a job past 45 s). It is session state, not a FreeCAD document change: FreeCAD's undo does not take it back.
flat_detect_edges.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

flat_curvature.description: Read how an edge bends, as ScanRuler's curvature comb draws it. Give chains or element, one of them. chains: edge chains by number, as flat_edges lists them (detected edges, or the cut of a section). element: a fitted 2D arc or circle, read exactly as 1/R. The answer for chains holds: unit, window, items [{ chain, closed, from, to (arc length along it), scatter, stretches [...] } or { chain, tooShort }]. The answer for an element holds: element, kind, unit, closed, from, to, stretches. A stretch is { kind: straight | arc | transition, from, to, start, end }. For an arc, it also holds radius (from its middle reading), radiusMin and radiusMax. On a section only, it holds convex: true for a round, false for the hollow of a fillet. The cut of a section knows its material side. A chain is read smoothed over window (2 sheet units by default, 0.2 to 20). One window is lost at each end of an open chain; a chain shorter than that answers tooShort. A sudden change becomes a transition about a window long, with the change in its middle. The tangent point of a fillet is the middle of the transition before it. A transition much longer than the window is a blend that is no arc. straightBelow (1/unit): curvature under it counts as straight. By default it is 0.002 or four times the scatter of the chain, whichever is larger. So on a noisy edge, a gentle round reads straight until straightBelow is given. tolerance (0.1): how far the readings of an arc may stray, as a share of its curvature. step adds samples [{ at, spot, curvature }] that far apart (at most 2000 a chain). Worked example: the cut of a Ø10 bore reads one arc, radius 4.99, convex false. A fitted circle of radius 8 reads one arc of radius 8, from 0 to just under its circumference, 50.27. comb: true also draws the comb into the FreeCAD document as a plain Part object of line segments. name: its name, or "Curvature comb". It lies on the plane of the section on the part, or on XY for an image. It is sized by scale (1) and spacing (a 150th of the extent of the edges, at least 0.2). That is one FreeCAD undo step. The answer then holds comb { object, teeth, mmPerCurvature, cap, spacing } and health. The object is a copy, not linked to the sheet. Without comb, it changes nothing. Refused: both or neither of chains and element. Refused: a chain number that the sheet does not have. Refused: an element that is a line or a point. Refused: comb with no document open (doc_new).
flat_curvature.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

flat_edges.description: List the edge chains of the sheet, longest first. Each holds { chain, points, length, closed, bounds { min, max } }, in the units of the sheet. chain is its number: what flat_fit, flat_profile and flat_curvature take. The numbers are NOT in this order. The answer also holds units and total. limit: how many are listed (50). The chains of an image are the detected edges (flat_detect_edges). Short specks at the diagonals of a hard edge can appear as extra chains. The chains of a section are the cut itself. A section has a point only where the cut crosses the edge of a triangle. So a straight side of a CAD-style mesh is 2 points. mesh_densify and mesh_use_edited before section_cut give more. Chain numbers change whenever edges are found again (flat_detect_edges, flat_calibrate, another image or section). Refused: nothing is on the sheet. Worked example: the middle cut of a 40 × 30 plate with a Ø10 hole. It lists a closed chain of length 140, and one of about 31.4. Changes nothing.
flat_edges.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

flat_fit.description: Make a 2D element on the sheet (kind point, line, circle or arc) by a method of that kind. Left out, the method is the edge method of the kind when chains or box is given. Else it is the pick method of the kind. Pick methods take points [[x, y], …]. flat-point-pick takes 1, flat-line-pick 2 or more, flat-circle-pick and flat-arc-pick 3 or more. Each point snaps to the nearest edge within reach (10 pixels' worth by default), unless snap: false. picks says where each landed { at, chain, moved }. Exactly the minimum goes through each point, so its sigma is 0. Edge methods (flat-line-edge, flat-circle-edge, flat-arc-edge) take chains and/or box. chains: whole chains by number, from flat_edges. box { min, max }: only the edge points inside it; alone, of every chain. They best-fit the points, with strays voted out: the usual way to measure. They need many points. So on a section of a mesh with few triangles, they fail with the count. Densify the mesh first, or pick points. Construct methods take refs: other 2D elements, by id or name. flat-point-midpoint: two points, circles or arcs (their centres). flat-point-intersect: two lines. flat-point-center: one circle, arc or point. flat-circle-centers: three or more; the circle through their centres. The seed methods (flat-line-seed, flat-circle-seed) are not ported, and they are refused. name: its name, else "Circle 1" and so on by kind. The answer holds: element { id, name, kind, fit }, and picks for a pick method. fit by kind: point { at }, line { center, dir, length }, circle { center, radius, zoneWidth }, arc { center, radius, start, sweep }. sweep is in radians, CCW from +X. Each fit has sigma (RMS), usedPoints and formError (peak to peak). Units are the sheet's: pixels on an uncalibrated image. An element is not a FreeCAD object; flat_export writes it out. Worked example: the edge of a disc of radius 8 at 10 px/mm. It fits the centre within 0.01, and radius 7.998. It is session state, not a FreeCAD document change: FreeCAD's undo does not take it back.
flat_fit.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

flat_dimension_add.description: Measure between two 2D elements. refs: two, each by id or name, in order. The types: flat-dist-point-point, flat-dist-point-line, flat-dist-line-line, flat-angle-line-line. flat-dist-point-point: centre distance, with ΔX and ΔY. flat-dist-point-line: the point first, then the line; the perpendicular distance. flat-dist-line-line: near-parallel lines only. Over 3° apart, the dimension is kept but reads invalid, saying to use the angle. A point, circle or arc counts as a point (its centre), and a line as a line. Without type, it takes the first type that takes the two in the order given. For two lines, that is the distance, so pass type for their angle. Refused, with the order of every type, when the two do not fit. For a line then a point: swap them. name: else "Distance 1" / "Angle 1". The value follows its elements: it is worked out on every read. It reads invalid once one element is removed. The answer holds: flat and report. flat: the 2D state: subject, units, calibration, edges, elements, dimensions [{ id, name, type, refs, value }]. report: the text that flat_report gives. Units are the sheet's: pixels when uncalibrated. Worked example: two fitted sides of a 10 × 6 rectangle read 5.97 to 6.00 apart. The centre of a circle to a side 13 away reads 13.000. It is session state, not a FreeCAD document change: FreeCAD's undo does not take it back.
flat_dimension_add.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

flat_note_add.description: Write a one-line text note on the 2D sheet. text: not empty. at: [x, y], its lower-left corner, in sheet units. flat_report lists it, and the SVG and DXF of flat_export hold it (as TEXT; Ø, ° and ± are spelled for DXF). flat_render does not draw it. A note keeps its place on the image when the sheet is calibrated again. It goes when another image or section takes the sheet. flat_edit { note } changes or hides it; flat_remove { notes } deletes it. Refused: nothing is on the sheet. The answer holds: note { id, text, at, visible }. It is session state, not a FreeCAD document change: FreeCAD's undo does not take it back.
flat_note_add.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

flat_edit.description: Change one thing on the 2D sheet. Give exactly one of element, dimension (each by id or name) or note (by id). When several are given, note wins, then element. An element or a dimension takes a new name. A note takes new text and/or a new place at. Any of them takes visible: false. That leaves an element or a note out of flat_export and flat_render. A hidden dimension is still listed in the report. It does not refit or move an element: use flat_remove and flat_fit again for that. Refused: none of the three given. Refused: an id or name that the sheet does not have. Refused: an empty name. The answer holds: for a note, { note }; otherwise the 2D state (subject, units, calibration, edges, elements, dimensions). It is session state, not a FreeCAD document change: FreeCAD's undo does not take it back.
flat_edit.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

flat_remove.description: Remove elements, dimensions and notes from the 2D sheet. elements and dimensions: each by id or name; notes: by id; any mix in one call. Nothing is removed when one of them is not found; the refusal names it. A dimension on a removed element stays and reads invalid (invalidDimensions lists it). Remove it too, or it shows as invalid in the report. Ids are not reused. The answer holds: the 2D state with what is left (elements, dimensions), removed { elements, dimensions, notes }. It also holds lostSource / invalidDimensions when they apply. It is session state, not a FreeCAD document change: FreeCAD's undo does not take it back.
flat_remove.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

flat_set_alignment.description: Put the zero point of the part at origin [x, y], and its X axis through xAxis [x, y]. These are two places on the sheet, in sheet units, and they must differ. flat_report and flat_export then read every place in that frame (y up, turned to match). The own inputs and answers of the tools (flat_fit, flat_edges, boxes, picks) stay in the frame of the sheet. clear: true takes the alignment off. It follows the image through flat_calibrate, and it goes with the subject of the sheet. The answer holds: the 2D state, and alignment { origin, angleDeg } when one is set. Worked example: origin at the lower-left corner of a rectangle [25, 10] and xAxis [35, 10] give angleDeg 0. A point at sheet [30, 13] then reports as X 5, Y 3. It is session state, not a FreeCAD document change: FreeCAD's undo does not take it back.
flat_set_alignment.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

flat_render.description: Make a picture of the 2D sheet as a PNG, in its own units, +X right and +Y up. It shows the image, the edge chains (teal), the visible elements in their colours, and a grid. path: where to write it (relative: the folder of the session; .png is added when missing). The default path is sheet.png there, written over each time. show picks the layers from image, edges, elements, grid (all by default). A section has no image; notes and dimensions are not drawn. frame { min, max } (sheet units) zooms in. A frame that lies off the sheet is refused, with the extent of the sheet. size: the long side in pixels (1200; 200 to 4000). The answer holds: file { path, name }, units, width, height (pixels), map { left, top, unitsPerPx, note }, and grid (its spacing). map: pixel (column c, row r from the top) is the sheet place [left + c·unitsPerPx, top − r·unitsPerPx]. The file is for looking at: open it, or send it to the person. The numbers come from flat_report. It needs the renderer of Agent Link (always there under Agent Link). It changes nothing on the sheet.
flat_render.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

flat_report.description: Read the 2D report as ScanRuler's Copy button gives it. The answer holds text and flat. text: the image (name, pixels) or the section (its name, scan and cut). text: the scale it rests on. That is the millimetres of a section, a measured calibration, or pixels. When only the own scale of the file is used, it says "UNCALIBRATED — nominal … dpi from file metadata". text: the coordinates (the alignment, when set). text: every element with its size and scatter (Ø for circles, L and angle for lines, X · Y for points). text: every dimension with its value, or why it is invalid, and the visible notes. flat: the 2D state as data (subject, image, units, calibration, edges { chains, sensitivity }, elements [{ id, name, kind, fit }], dimensions [{ id, name, type, refs, value }]). The fits of the state are in the frame of the sheet. The places of the text are in the frame of the alignment, when one is set. Refused: nothing is on the sheet. Changes nothing.
flat_report.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

flat_export.description: Write the sheet at true scale for CAD or a laser. format dxf: AutoCAD 2000, millimetres declared, y up. In DXF, the edge chains are LWPOLYLINE thinned to 0.01 mm, and fits are LINE / CIRCLE / ARC / POINT. Their labels and the notes are TEXT. format svg: one unit a millimetre, y down. path: where to write (relative: the folder of the session; the extension of the format is added when missing). Left out, path is <image name or section name>.<format> in the folder of the session, written over when there. It writes every chain, every visible element with a fit, and every visible note. They are in the frame of the alignment, when one is set (flat_set_alignment). Trap: on an uncalibrated image the units are pixels, and the "millimetres" of the file are pixels. Use flat_calibrate first; units in the answer says which. Refused: nothing is on the sheet. Refused: the path cannot be written. The answer holds: file { path, name, bytes }, format, units, elements, chains (counts written). It changes nothing on the sheet. To get a section into the FreeCAD model instead, use section_to_sketch.
flat_export.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/flat.py

deviation_open_reference.description: Open the nominal part that the scan is compared with, in place of the one there is. It needs a scan open. Inputs: path or body, one of them. path: a STEP, IGES or BREP from CAD, tessellated finely (0.002 to 0.01 mm off the surface, by size). path can also be an STL, PLY, OBJ, OFF or 3MF mesh. It can also be glTF/GLB, Collada, VRML or 3DS, where Agent Link reads them. body: a shape in the FreeCAD document, by name or label, tessellated the same way, as it stands now. A later change to the body is not followed: open it again. units: mm (default), cm, m or in, for mesh files; a CAD file carries its own. Gotchas: any alignment and map against the old reference go. The reference is taken in its own coordinates. So a body inside a moved container is read where its own Placement puts it. An open reference (warnings: n open edges) cannot give a trusted sign near its holes. A reference mesh is welded, and turned outward if it came inside out. Size: the fine tessellation of a large or very curved CAD part makes a large mesh, and it takes time. It runs on the own thread of the window (not measured). The answer holds: deviation { source, reference { fileName, triangles, volume mm³, openEdges }, align: null, map: "none", settings } and warnings. The reference of a file is put in the document as a mesh object; a body stays itself. Next: deviation_align. It keeps the reference in ScanRuler's state; the model is not changed.
deviation_open_reference.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/deviation.py

deviation_align.description: Make a rigid best fit (no scale) of the scan onto the reference, then the deviation map under it. It needs deviation_open_reference. Inputs: mode auto (default), points or local. auto finds the pose on its own. points starts from pairs: three or more { scan: [x, y, z], reference: [x, y, z] } of the same places, not in a line; then it refines. local refines the fit in hand on a marked surface only: vertices, within searchDistance mm. allowSizeMismatch: true, only for a scan that truly is a small piece of the reference. What it does: the scan, with every element measured on it, is MOVED onto the reference. In FreeCAD, the Placement of the scan object follows. Every coordinate afterwards is in the frame of the reference. Gotchas: read warnings every time. Each of these means that the map is not to be trusted as it stands. That is: a matchedShare under 50 %, a fit that did not converge, or under 80 % of the points measured. Or: ambiguous, a part with a symmetry, where two poses fit equally; give pairs. Refused (invalid_input): the scan and the reference differ in size by more than 2×. That is a unit mix-up, named when near ×10, ×25.4 or ×1000. Refused: vertices that are not numbers. Moving the part afterwards (align_clear, align_datum, align_auto, align_symmetry, scan_scale) drops this alignment and its map. On a scan with no noise, the automatic colour range comes out near zero: set deviation_settings { range }. Sign: positive where the scan stands outside the reference (excess material on the part). Negative where it stands inside it (material missing). The automatic search distance is 2 % of the diagonal of the reference. Readings past it count as unmeasured. The answer holds: deviation { align { source, rms, meanDistance, matched, sampled, iterations, converged, matchedShare, ambiguous, pairRms, transform }, map, sign, stats { min, max, mean, rms, sigma, percentiles, measured, total, withinTolerancePct, withinToleranceOfMeasuredPct, measuredPct }, settings }, moved, warnings. withinTolerancePct is over every scan point, measured or not. Size: 25,000 sampled points drive the fit, then every vertex is measured. At 137,000 triangles: 32 s for auto, 9 s from points. That is plain Python off the Mac; the Mac is not measured. Declared heavy: on its own it runs as a job. Past 45 s, the call answers with a job id: job_status { job } gives the answer. It keeps the result in ScanRuler's state; the model is not changed.

allowSizeMismatch.description: Fit even when the scan and the reference differ in size by more than 2× — only for a scan that truly is a small piece of a larger reference, never to get past a unit mix-up.

reference.description: The same point on the reference, mm.

deviation_align.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/deviation.py

deviation_measure.description: Measure the deviation map again under the alignment in hand. Use it after an element target, or to be sure that it is of the reference. deviation_align measures it already, and deviation_settings { facingDeg } measures again itself. So this is seldom needed. No inputs. Refused (invalid_state): there is no reference, or no alignment. That is: never aligned, or the part was moved since; align_clear, align_datum, align_auto, align_symmetry, scan_scale drop it. Then run deviation_align again. The answer holds: deviation { source: "reference", align, stats { min, max, mean, rms, sigma, percentiles p5 … p95, measured, total, withinTolerancePct (over every scan point), withinToleranceOfMeasuredPct, measuredPct }, settings }. It holds warnings when under 80 % of the points have a reading within the search distance. Sign: positive where the scan stands outside the reference (excess material), negative inside it (material missing). Size: every scan vertex is measured against the reference. 6.5 s at 68,000 vertices (plain Python off the Mac; the Mac not measured). Declared heavy: on its own it runs as a job. It keeps the map in ScanRuler's state; the model is not changed.
deviation_measure.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/deviation.py

deviation_set_target.description: Map how far the scan strays from one of its own fitted elements, instead of from a reference part. The element is a plane, cylinder, sphere or torus. This gives the flatness of a face or the roundness of a bore as a map. Inputs: element (needed): id or name, or null to go back to the map of the reference part. side: outward or inward. outward: the outer side of the element is the outside of the material (a shaft, a top face). inward: a bore, a shell. Left out, side is read off the scan; give it to override. facingDeg (60; 1 to 90, or null for any): only surface that faces the element within that many degrees counts. No reference or alignment is needed. Gotchas: only the part of the scan near and facing the element is measured. So measuredPct is small, and withinTolerancePct, which counts every scan point, is small with it. Read withinToleranceOfMeasuredPct. The map replaces the map of the reference for deviation_hotspots, deviation_export and scan_heightmap { of: "deviation" }. That holds until element: null. Removing the element clears it. Sign: positive past the surface of the element on the outer side of the material (too much material). Negative short of it. The answer holds: deviation { source: "element", target { element, side, facingDeg }, stats, settings }. Size: every vertex is read (0.06 s at 68,000, plain Python off the Mac). Declared heavy: on its own it runs as a job. It keeps the map in ScanRuler's state.

element.description: The element (id or name), or null.

deviation_set_target.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/deviation.py

deviation_settings.description: Set how the deviation map is read; with nothing, it reads the settings. Inputs: tolerance: ± mm that the statistics count within; 0.1 by default. maxDistance: the search distance, mm; readings past it count as unmeasured. By default, maxDistance is 2 % of the diagonal of the reference. range: the colour scale, ± mm; by default from the map. On a scan without noise, range is near zero by default, so set it then. bands: 2 to 256 colour steps, or null for a smooth scale. facingDeg: 1 to 90, or null; 90 by default. facingDeg: how far the surface of the scan may face away from the reference, and still count. colormap: jet. Gotchas: facingDeg measures the map again at once (as long as deviation_measure). maxDistance and tolerance change how the map in hand is counted, not its values. A too short maxDistance shows as a low measuredPct. Setting range or maxDistance turns their automatic values off. The answer holds: deviation { source, reference, align, map, sign, stats, target, settings { range, maxDistance, maxDistanceAuto, bands, tolerance, facingDeg, colormap } }. It keeps the settings in ScanRuler's state; the model is not changed.
deviation_settings.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/deviation.py

deviation_hotspots.description: Read the deviation map as patches, in a few rows: where the part is wrong. The vertices past the tolerance are gathered into connected regions, the largest and farthest first. It needs a map (deviation_align or deviation_set_target). Inputs: tolerance: the map's by default. patches: 8; 50 at most. grain: mm, how far apart two points may be and still join; three point spacings by default. on: scan (default) or reference. The answer (on scan) holds: source, tolerance, over (vertices past it), found, features { count, shareOfExcess }, spacing, grain, patches, far and unmeasured. Each patch: centroid, box, area mm², count, mean, extreme, depth, volume, kind, side, at, vertex, vertices. depth: the median |deviation|. volume: mm³ past the tolerance; the ranking key. kind "feature": at least 4 mm² and 25 point spacings², and a depth of 2× the tolerance. A feature is material missing or misplaced, to model or to name; else kind is "texture". at and vertex: the place of the extreme. Gotchas: read far every time: the vertices past the search distance, left out of the patches. far.inside is scan deep inside the reference: a hole, pocket or slot that the model lacks. far.outside is scan standing off it. area and volume come from the point spacing, and they run a little over on a densified CAD mesh. Sign: mean and extreme are positive (side outside) where the scan stands outside the reference: excess material. They are negative (side inside) where material is missing. on: reference reads the map on the reference instead, signed the same way. It then holds coveredPct, withinTolerancePct over the area of the reference, mostExcess, mostMissing and unscanned. unscanned: reference surface with no scan facing it. It casts a reading for every small piece of the reference against the triangles of the scan. There are 200,000 pieces at most; spacing says how fine. That is slow: minutes on a 137,000-triangle scan in plain Python off the Mac (the Mac not measured). It is kept afterwards, until the map or the settings change. Ask for it only when unscanned areas matter. Declared heavy: on its own it runs as a job, and job_status { job } gives the answer. on scan answers in under a second. Changes nothing.
deviation_hotspots.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/deviation.py

deviation_volume.description: Compare the scan and the reference part as solids, on a grid of small cells. Each cell inside one and not the other is an error; touching cells are a region. It needs deviation_align. Inputs: tolerance: the map's by default. A cell within tolerance of the surface of the scan is noise, never an error. cell: mm; by default from the tolerance and the size of the part. The default is widened to keep 16 million cells at most. within { min, max } limits it to a box. regions: 8; 50 at most. kinds: any of excess, missing, unsure. TRAP: the words run the other way from the words of the map. Here excess is material that the REFERENCE has and the part has not. That is: the model is too big there (a dent, a worn face, a pocket not modelled). missing is material that the part has and the reference lacks (a boss or lump to add to the model). unsure is where an open scan does not say; it is never an error. On the map and in deviation_hotspots, "excess" means the opposite: the scan outside the reference. Other gotchas: nothing thinner than smallestSeen (two cells) is seen. An open scan gives scanOpen and unsure regions. An open reference gives referenceOpen and a warning. The answer holds: tolerance, cell, smallestSeen, modelVolume mm³, totals { excess, missing, unsure: { volume mm³, share % of the reference } }, found, regions, seconds. regions, largest first: { kind, volume, maxDepth, thickness, shape layer | lump, centroid, deepest, box, evidence, confidence }. Size: the cost goes with the cell count, not with the scan. 2.6 s for a 60 mm part at a 0.24 mm cell (plain Python off the Mac). Declared heavy: on its own it runs as a job, and job_status { job } gives the answer. It keeps the result for the panel; the model is not changed.
deviation_volume.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/deviation.py

deviation_export.description: Write the deviation map as a file. It needs a map (deviation_align or deviation_set_target). Inputs: format ply (default), csv, npy or report. ply: binary, a vertex per scan vertex, with x, y, z, deviation, measured and the jet colour of the map. csv: x,y,z,d. npy: N × 4 float32. report: ScanRuler's plain-text report, also in the answer. side: scan (default) or reference. reference: the map read on the reference, a reading per small piece of it; ply, csv or npy only. path: a relative name goes in the folder of the session. Left out, path is <scan>-deviation-<side>.<format> there, and .txt for the report. The answer holds: side, format, readings, measured, measuredPct, withinTolerance, withinTolerancePct, withinToleranceOfMeasuredPct, tolerance, searchDistance, file (the path), and report with its text. withinTolerancePct is over every reading, measured or not. Gotchas: the distance is NaN where there is no reading. A reading past the search distance is kept as it is; measured says which count. Coordinates are in the frame of the reference, where the alignment put the scan. Sign, both sides: positive where the scan stands outside the reference (excess material), negative inside it (material missing). Size: side scan writes at once (about 20 bytes a vertex in PLY). side reference first reads the map on the reference. That is the slow reading that deviation_hotspots { on: "reference" } describes (minutes; kept for the next call). Declared heavy: on its own it runs as a job. Changes nothing in the document.
deviation_export.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/deviation.py

thickness_measure.description: Measure the wall thickness at the points of the scan, with no reference. It measures from each point along the inward normal to the far wall. Each input is kept for later calls. method: ray (default) or sphere (the largest sphere that fits at the point). maxThickness: mm, the thickest wall searched for; by default a fifth of the diagonal of the scan. A wall thicker than that reads as unmeasured: raise it to read the size of a solid block. coneRays: 0 is one ray; more takes the shortest of a cone. coneAngleDeg: 30. normalDeviationDeg: 60, or null; how far the far wall may turn from facing back. maxPoints: 300,000; 0 for all. A larger scan is measured at that many points, spread evenly. The others take the thinnest reading among their neighbours. The answer holds: thickness { status, stats { measured, total, min, max, mean, rms, sigma, belowLimit, limit, belowLimitPct }, settings, sampled { points, of } }, thinSpots and report. thinSpots { count, found, patches thinnest first: centroid, box, count, area, minThickness, meanThickness, at, vertex, vertices }. thinSpots are the points under the thin-wall limit (1 mm; thickness_settings { limit }). report: the plain text. Gotchas: thinSpots.count counts every scan point under the limit. The unmeasured points count with the reading that they took from a neighbour. So it can be several times stats.belowLimit (measured points only) when maxPoints sampled the scan. Thin readings along open rims are rays escaping, not thin walls. On a solid block, the reading across a corner is the distance to the next face met, not a wall. The statistics are over the points measured only. Refused: no wall is found within maxThickness anywhere. Size: a ray for every measured point, walked through a grid of cells over the mesh. So only the triangles near its path are tried. Measured live before the grid: 221 s on the Mac. That was for 20,000 points at 25 mm on 219,600 triangles. Then every leaf of triangles that a run of rays swept was tried. The same reading with the grid takes 0.4 s, where it was 66 s, in a Linux container. The Mac is not measured since. Cost grows with the points measured and with maxThickness (the cells that each ray crosses). maxPoints 20,000 reads the walls of a part well. Declared heavy: on its own it runs as a job. Past 45 s, the call answers with a job id: job_status { job } gives the answer. It keeps the map in ScanRuler's state (view_render { map: "thickness" } shows it), and FreeCAD's Save carries it. A document opened again still has it. A map taken before the scan was moved or scaled is dropped, not kept. The model is not changed.

maxPoints.description: Most vertices measured; a bigger scan is sampled evenly to this many and the rest read off their neighbours. 300000 by default, 0 for every vertex.

maxThickness.description: The thickest wall searched for, mm.

method.description: ray: along the inward normal to the far wall (the shortest of a cone with coneRays). sphere: the largest sphere that fits at the point.

normalDeviationDeg.description: How far the far wall may turn from facing back, degrees, or null for any.

thickness_measure.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/thickness.py

thickness_settings.description: Set the wall-thickness settings; with nothing, it reads them. Search settings: method, maxThickness, coneRays, coneAngleDeg, normalDeviationDeg, maxPoints, as thickness_measure takes them. They take effect at the next thickness_measure, not on the map in hand. Reading settings act at once. low and high: the ends of the colour scale, mm; setting one turns the automatic scale off. bands: 2 or more colour steps, or null. limit: the thin-wall limit that the statistics count under, mm; 1 by default. The answer holds: thickness { status ready | none, stats, settings }. When limit was given and there is a map, it also holds thinSpots under the new limit. It keeps the settings in ScanRuler's state; the model is not changed.

maxPoints.description: Most vertices measured; a bigger scan is sampled evenly to this many and the rest read off their neighbours. 300000 by default, 0 for every vertex.

maxThickness.description: The thickest wall searched for, mm.

method.description: ray: along the inward normal to the far wall (the shortest of a cone with coneRays). sphere: the largest sphere that fits at the point.

normalDeviationDeg.description: How far the far wall may turn from facing back, degrees, or null for any.

thickness_settings.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/thickness.py

scan_noise.description: Measure the own noise of this scan. It is the median scatter of small plane fits over 4,000 sampled places (sigmaMm). It also gives p90, and spacingMm (the median edge length). It is kept with the scan as its measured noise. No inputs. The answer holds: sigmaMm, p90, spacingMm, sampled, next, and plan. plan: the noise to plan with. It is the larger of the usual noise of the named scanner and the noise of this scan. plan { sigmaMm, source profile | measured, from, finestMm, warning }. finestMm: three times the noise; nothing finer is to be trusted or modelled. warning: when no scanner is named, or the scan reads 1.5× its scanner or more. scan_thread, wear_diff and fit_scan_measure read plan. Gotchas: refused for a CAD tessellation; it has no scan noise, and its numbers are exact. A CAD tessellation has half or more of its vertices between exactly coplanar triangles. A textured or knurled surface reads as noise. scanner { action: "use" } names the known figure of the scanner instead. scan_qa gives the same median beside its other checks. It keeps the reading in ScanRuler's state; the model is not changed.
scan_noise.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/noise.py

scanner.description: Keep your scanners across projects, in scanners.json in the folder of the session. Each scanner: { name, noiseMm, spacingMm, note }. noiseMm: one standard deviation of its usual noise, over 0 to 5 mm. action (needed): list, add, remove, use, export or import. add { scanner: { name, noiseMm, spacingMm?, note? }, use?: true }: a scanner of that name is replaced. remove { name }. use { name } names the scanner that this scan came from. use { measured: true } names none; the plan then rests on scan_noise alone. export { path? }: scanners-export.json in the folder of the session by default. import { path }: merged by name, and the entries of the file win. The answer for list holds: scanners, using, measured, file. The answer for each other action holds what it did. Each answer also holds plan: the noise to plan with ({ sigmaMm, source, from, finestMm, warning }). plan is null, with a note, when no scanner is named and nothing is measured. scan_thread, wear_diff and fit_scan_measure read plan. Gotchas: the choice is kept with the scan by value. So removing or editing a scanner afterwards does not change a project that named it. The figure of a scanner is what it usually gives on a flat, matte part, not its catalogue accuracy. It writes scanners.json (and the export file); the model is not changed.
scanner.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/noise.py

scan_thread.description: Name a scanned thread. The points about the axis of a cylinder are read for pitch, crests and roots, and the hand. Then they are folded along the helix, for a sharper pitch, starts, the flank angle and the taper. The result is decided against ISO metric, UNC, UNF, UNEF, NPT, G/R pipe, Tr, ACME and the 45° print form. Inputs: axis (needed): { element } or { origin, direction, radius, length? } in mm. element: a cylinder fitted in the bore or on the boss (element_fit kind cylinder). Give that fit radius or side, so it lands on the thread, not on the wall beside it. band: mm either side of the radius that a point counts; max(0.6, 0.2 × radius). length: mm along the axis, centred on its origin; the length of the cylinder by default. families: which to try; all by default. pitchFloor: 0.01, the least share that a pitch is resolved to. Raise pitchFloor for a scanner whose scale you trust less. detail: full adds candidates and the tooth profile. The answer holds verdict: match (with confidence high or low), ambiguous, or none. ambiguous: tied; the sizes that this scan cannot tell apart. deciding: the hand measurement that would tell them apart, and what each reads. The answer also holds: best { designation, family, form, major, pitch, tpi, angle, taper, pitchOff, diameterOff }, ruledOut, reads, scanNoise, tolerance, note, next. reads { pitch, pitchSigma, tpi, major, minor, internal, leftHanded, starts, lead, flankAngle, flankConfidence, taper, noise, length, points }. note: the verdict in words. A plain wall answers verdict none with thread: false. Gotchas: a bore is matched on its crests (the minor diameter), a boss on its own (the major). The diameter tolerance widens with the noise to plan with (scan_noise, scanner). So a noisy scanner ties sizes that it cannot resolve. Ask the person for the deciding measurement, rather than pick. Size: at most 200,000 points are read (every k-th past that). 0.25 s on a plain bore (plain Python off the Mac). It notes the result in ScanRuler's state; the model is not changed.

axis.description: { element } — a cylinder fitted in the bore or on the boss (element_fit kind cylinder) — or { origin, direction, radius, length? }.

band.description: mm either side of the radius a point counts; max(0.6, 0.2·radius) by default.

families.description: Families to try: metric, unc, unf, unef, npt, bspp, bspt, tr, acme, print45; all by default.

length.description: mm along the axis, centred on its origin; the cylinder's length by default.

scan_thread.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/thread.py

wear_setup.description: Set the settings, tags and the reference for wear repair, in one call; with nothing, it reads them. Inputs: tolerance (0.05 mm): what counts as worn, and the target of the pre-warp. blendMm (1): how far outside a worn region a repair fades out. maxMm (2): how far the reference may be, and still be the same surface. mode: add (default: only lost material comes back) or both (what stands proud is trimmed too). reset: true puts these four back, and it wins over values given in the same call. tag: [{ action set | remove | clear, name, kind worn | keep, region }]. region: { kind: "box", min, max } or { kind: "sphere", center, radius }, in the frame that the part is measured in now. keep is never moved: a fit face, a datum, a feature meant to differ from the other half. A tag of a name in use replaces it. reference: { source: "mirror", plane: "x" | "y" | "z" }: the own other half of the part across that coordinate plane, through the zero point. Use align_symmetry first, so the mirror plane is one of them. reference: { source: "mirror", point, normal }. reference: { source: "deviation" }: the reference part, as the scan is aligned to it. Use deviation_open_reference and deviation_align first, or it is refused. Gotchas: regions are boxes and spheres in current coordinates, and they do not follow the part. Tag after aligning, and tag again after any move. A mirror reference repairs only damage that the other half does not share. The answer holds: settings, tags, reference. Then wear_diff. It keeps them in ScanRuler's state; the model is not changed.

region.description: { kind: box, min, max } or { kind: sphere, center, radius }, in the frame the part is measured in now.

wear_setup.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/wear.py

wear_diff.description: Read how worn each region tagged worn is, against the reference chosen in wear_setup. Input: names: only these worn regions; all by default. The answer holds: reference, tolerance, regions, scatter, scanNoise, floor and note. regions: name, points, lost, added, mean, rms, pointsLost and pointsAdded. lost: the deepest that the scan stands in from the reference, negative mm. added: the most that it stands out. pointsLost and pointsAdded: points past the tolerance either way. scatter: the own spread of the scan against the reference, off the worn regions. scanNoise: the noise to plan with (scan_noise, scanner). floor: the least tolerance that they support: twice the scatter or three times the noise, the larger. note comes when the tolerance is under floor. Then the wear read is partly noise: raise wear_setup { tolerance }. Gotchas: a point further than maxMm from the reference is not counted. A piece broken off reads as nothing there, not as deep wear. The mean is over every point in the region, worn or not. Refused: no region is tagged worn, or no reference is chosen (wear_setup). Refused: the deviation reference is no longer aligned. Every vertex is read against the reference: 1.4 s at 68,000 vertices (plain Python off the Mac). Changes nothing.
wear_diff.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/wear.py

wear_rebuild.description: Write the scan with each worn region brought back onto the reference. Every vertex there is moved to the reference, fading out over blendMm outside the region. It is never moved inside a keep region, and never where the reference is past maxMm. Inputs: names: only these worn regions. mode: add or both (the mode of wear_setup by default). path: an STL; a relative name goes in the folder of the session. Left out, path is <scan>-repaired.stl there. The answer holds: file { path, name, bytes }, moved (vertices), largestMoveMm, before and after per region { name, lost, added, pointsLost }, note, next. Gotchas: it writes a file, and leaves the open scan as it is. scan_open the file (discard: true) to measure the repair, or import_file to bring it into the document. A dent comes back; a piece broken off (no scan surface there) does not: model that from the reference. The mesh keeps the triangles of the scan, so it is as open or closed as the scan was. Coordinates are those that the part is measured in now. A binary STL is 50 bytes a triangle (6.8 MB for 137,000). It changes nothing in the session or the document.
wear_rebuild.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/wear.py

wear_prewarp.description: Pre-warp a model against a print of it. Set-up: the target (the CAD, or a repaired part) is open as the deviation reference. A scan of a print of it is the scan, aligned (deviation_align). Else it is refused. The target is moved back at every point by the error that the print shows there. The error is smoothed over smooth neighbour rings (2; 0 to 10), so scan scatter is not printed in. It is multiplied by gain (1; 0.2 to 1.5). The result is written as an STL in the own frame of the target, to print next. Inputs: gain, smooth. fresh: true starts the run count again. path: an STL; left out, <target>-prewarp-<run>.stl in the folder of the session. The answer holds: file, run, rms, largest, unread, seenFromPrint { largest, rms }, runs [{ run, rms }], stop, why, warning and note. rms: the error of this print against the target, mm. unread: target points with no scan within the maxMm of wear_setup. seenFromPrint: the same error, read from the own points of the print to the target. stop is true once the print is within the tolerance. stop is also true when a run gained less than a fifth on the one before. stop is also true when three runs are made. Gotchas: the error is read, and corrected, at the own vertices of the target only. A target tessellated from CAD has its vertices on its edges and rims. So an error in the middle of a face reads rms 0 there. The own points of the print can lie further off than the tolerance. They can also lie further off than anything that the vertices of the target show. Then the answer holds warning, and stop is false. Open the target again as a mesh fine enough to carry the error. Each call counts as a run, so call it once per scanned print. The written mesh is the tessellation of the reference, moved; it is not a CAD solid. It corrects shape error that repeats from print to print, not warping that differs each time. Starting the print is the call of the person. It notes the run in ScanRuler's state; the model is not changed.
wear_prewarp.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/wear.py

catalog_part.description: Find standard parts offline, with nominal dimensions in mm. The parts: socket head and button head screws, hex nuts, washers and deep-groove bearings. There are three uses. designation: the sizes of a part by name. Examples: "M5 socket head", "608", "M8 washer", "M4" for every M4 part, "ISO 4762" for a standard. limit: 20 by default, 100 at most. The answer then holds parts [{ designation, kind, standard, dims }]. dims (kind narrows it): the sizes measured, by the own names of each kind. The names for screws: [d, dk, k, s]. For nuts: [d, s, m]. For washers: [d1, d2, h]. For bearings: [d, D, B]. Each is matched as a share of its nominal. The answer then holds matches [{ designation, kind, standard, dims, agree [{ dim, nominal, measured, off }], worst }]. limit is 5 by default. named comes when one part fits within 5 %, and clearly better than the next. Else note says which two tie and what else to measure, or that nothing is within 5 %. Neither: the answer holds the kinds and their dimension names. Gotchas: the names in dims are case-sensitive (bearing D and d differ). A scanned size carries the noise of the scan: measure diameters with element_fit, not from two points. The table is small, so no match is not proof that the part is special. It needs no scan and no document. Changes nothing.
catalog_part.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/catalog.py

catalog_links.description: Search pages for the CAD of a part on the catalogues and model libraries, for the person to open. Nothing is fetched or downloaded from here. Inputs: query (needed): a designation or description. sources: any of traceparts, mcmaster, misumi, printables, thangs, grabcad (all by default). An unknown source is refused with the list. The answer holds: links [{ source, label, kind catalogue | library, url, terms }] and note. terms: what the source allows for a downloaded model, in a line. Next: the person downloads a file, and import_file brings it into the document. catalog_provenance { action: "record" } notes where it came from, so pack_plan knows whether it may be passed on. Changes nothing.
catalog_links.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/catalog.py

catalog_provenance.description: Keep where each file brought into the project came from, in provenance.json in the folder of the session. Inputs: action list (default) or record. record { file, source (both needed), page, licence, shareable }. A record of a file name already there replaces it, and the date is added (at). shareable: false keeps the file out of anything that pack_write shares; it is linked in the README instead. The answer holds: files [{ file, source, page, licence, shareable, at }], path, note. pack_setup takes these records as the upstream parts of the pack, until upstream is set there. It writes provenance.json; the model is not changed.
catalog_provenance.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/catalog.py

manual_plan.description: Keep the plan of the assembly manual as data with the project; with nothing, it reads it. Inputs: settings { title, explode, view, product, version, publisher, safety, intendedUse, disposal }. explode: how far new parts are drawn out along their move, a share of their travel (1). style { name, custom, words }. name: ste100 (default: short sentences, one instruction each, the verb first), plain or custom. custom: your own rules as Markdown lines ("maxWords: 25", "passive: off", "- avoid -> use"). words: the word list of the project. parts [{ name, body, kind part | hardware, designation, source, qty }]. body: the label of a body in the document. A part of a name in use is replaced. fromBodies: true adds every body that is not yet a part. removeParts: [names]. steps: the whole list, which replaces the list in hand. step [{ … }]: each step is added, or it replaces the step of the same id. at is a position from 1. A step holds: id, place, sub, tools, torque, warnings, text, notes, view. place [{ part, move, travel }]. move: the direction that the part moves in to its place; [0, 0, -1] by default. travel: mm; clear of itself by default. sub: build a sub-assembly apart, under this name; a later step places it by that name. warnings [{ level danger | warning | caution | notice, text }]. export: a file path to write the plan as JSON. import: a file path to read; it replaces the plan in hand. Gotchas: parts are placed where their bodies stand in the document, so the model must be assembled. A step that names a part that is not listed is reported under problems. Parts that no step places are under unplaced. Hardware without a body is listed, but not drawn or checked. The answer holds: settings, style, parts, steps, problems, unplaced, exported. Then manual_check, then manual_render. It keeps the plan in ScanRuler's state; the model is not changed.
manual_plan.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/manual.py

manual_check.description: Check the manual before you render it. Each part is swept in along its move against the parts already there, at 17 places along its travel. The parts already there are those in its sub-assembly, or in the main one. Each placement reads overlapsInPlace, blockedShortBy or clear. overlapsInPlace: it sits in another part where it ends. That is an interference fit, or the model is wrong: read it first; the way in is then not swept. blockedShortBy: mm; it is clear where it sits, but it runs into a part that far short of its place. Then use another way in, or an earlier step. The words of each step are linted to the style: length, passive, one instruction, the verb first, the word list. No inputs. The answer holds: steps [{ step, parts [{ part, clear | blockedShortBy | overlapsInPlace, note, move, travel, checked, why }], lint }], blocked, lintFindings, problems, unplaced. blocked: how many placements are blocked or overlap. Gotchas: an overlap under a ten-thousandth of the volume of the part is let through, so touching faces are clear. A body over 5,000 faces (a mesh brought in as a solid) is named as not checked. Hardware without a body is not checked. The sweep is straight, along move only. Size: up to 17 boolean cuts of FreeCAD's kernel for each placed part, against everything in place. So it grows with parts × their faces; not measured. It is declared heavy, so on its own it runs as a job. job_status { job } gives the answer past 45 s. Refused: no steps. Changes nothing.
manual_check.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/manual.py

manual_render.description: Write the manual as one HTML page, with its pictures inside. It holds the parts list, then the picture of each step. In a picture, parts in place are grey. The own parts of the step are in colour, drawn out along their moves, with arrows in. Each step also has its parts, tools, torque, safety messages and words. Inputs: width (900) and height (640) of each picture, in pixels (200 to 2000). path: an .html file; a relative name goes in the folder of the session. Left out, path is <title>.html there. The answer holds: file { path, name, bytes }, steps, pictures, lint (the style findings per step), note. Print it to PDF from a browser. Gotchas: it does not check the ways in: use manual_check first. A step whose view is not one of the views of the renderer is refused, naming them. Agent Link's own renderer draws the pictures from the shapes of the bodies (0.1 mm tessellation), not from the window. Size: a picture a step. It is declared heavy, so on its own it runs as a job. job_status { job } gives the answer past 45 s. Not measured. Refused: no steps. Changes nothing in the document.
manual_render.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/manual.py

pack_setup.description: Set the library pack: the design made ready to share; with nothing, it reads it. Inputs: title, author (the copyright holder), summary, printSettings (free text). licence: an id, or as a page wrote it ("CC BY-SA"). The ids: CC-BY-4.0, CC-BY-SA-4.0, CC-BY-NC-4.0, CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0, CC-BY-ND-4.0, CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0, CC0-1.0, MIT, GPL-3.0-only or ARR (all rights reserved). An unknown licence is refused with the list. includeStep and include3mf: true. renders: 0 to 6 pictures; 4. bodies: labels; every body by default. files: paths of files to add (a sliced 3MF, photos, the HTML of the manual); each must exist. Each file must be in the folder of the session. Refused: a file outside that folder, a hidden file or folder, a printer file (printers.json), and Agent Link's own state. To add another file, the person copies it into the folder of the session first. upstream: the parts taken from others: [{ part, body?, title, author, url, licence, source, redistribute, modified, permission }]. Until upstream is set here, the records of catalog_provenance are used. The answer holds: settings, bodies, files, upstream, licences (the ids with their short names), note. Then pack_plan says whether it can go out, and pack_write writes it. It keeps the pack in ScanRuler's state; the model is not changed.
pack_setup.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/pack.py

pack_plan.description: Check whether the pack can go out under its licence. No inputs. Each upstream part is checked against the licence of the pack. credited: with what the pack must carry for it. blocked: with why (a licence that does not allow it, share-alike that does not match, no licence known). leftOut: from a source whose terms do not allow passing files on; linked in the README instead of packed. problems: what is missing (no author, no title …). The answer holds: ok, licence, problems, credited, blocked, leftOut, bodies, files, note. pack_write refuses while ok is false. It is a guide from the terms of each licence as commonly read, not legal advice. The person confirms each upstream licence. Changes nothing.
pack_plan.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/pack.py

pack_write.description: Write the pack as a zip. It holds: models/ (STL of each body, and 3MF and STEP when asked), images/ (renders), files/, README.md with attribution, LICENSE. Input: path: a .zip; a relative name goes in the folder of the session. Left out, path is <title>.zip there. Every file is scrubbed first, and each kind of change is reported. The scrub takes out absolute paths and the user name in them. It takes out access codes, keys, tokens, printer serials and addresses, and e-mails. A field named only key, token, password or secret is emptied too. It also takes out the author of a STEP header, the text of an STL header, and picture metadata. The answer holds: file { path, name, bytes }, contents, scrubbed [{ what, count }], credited, leftOut, note. Gotchas: refused while pack_plan says that it cannot go out; the message lists why. Refused: no body to pack. Bodies of upstream parts that may not be passed on are left out. The scrub is by pattern. The person reads README.md and looks over the files before uploading, and the upload is theirs to do. Size: FreeCAD meshes and exports each body, and draws each render, on the own thread of the window. That is not measured; many bodies or 6 renders take a while. Changes nothing in the document.
pack_write.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/pack.py

fit_scan_setup.description: Set how a scanned print is read against the CAD that it was printed from. With nothing, it reads the settings. Inputs: up: which way of the CAD stood up on the bed: +z (default), -z, +x, -x, +y, -y. band (1 mm): how far off the surface a point still counts. footBand (0.2): the height of the first layer. footAbove (2.5): where the wall is read, to compare the foot with. slicer: the key map: bambustudio (default), orcaslicer, prusaslicer, or one of your own. current { key: value }: the values of the slicer in use, which the changes are added to. inner [wall ids]: walls of pockets, which take the hole offset. ignore [feature ids]: left out. keymap { id, label, keys: { contour | hole | foot | scaleXY | scaleZ: { key, kind add | percentMeasured | percentShrink | objectScale | unsupported, sign?, section?, note? } } } adds your own map. Your map is kept in fit-keymaps.json in the folder of the session. removeKeymap: its id. Feature ids (+X1, -Z2, H1, B1) come from fit_scan_features. The answer holds: settings, keymaps [{ id, label, checked }], runs. It keeps the settings in ScanRuler's state; the model is not changed.
fit_scan_setup.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/fitcomp.py

fit_scan_features.description: List the features of the reference that the print will be read on. They are in the build frame (up as fit_scan_setup has it). It needs the CAD open as the deviation reference, and the scan aligned to it (deviation_open_reference, deviation_align). Else it is refused. No inputs. The answer holds: planes, circles, zMin, zMax, inner, note. planes: flat walls, floors and tops square to an axis. Each plane: { id (+X1, -X1, +Z1 … numbered along the axis), axis, sign, offset mm, area, min, max }. circles: upright holes and bosses. Each circle: { id H1 … or B1 …, kind hole | boss, center, radius, zMin, zMax, coverage° }. Use it to choose what to tag. The walls of a pocket go in fit_scan_setup { inner }: they take the hole offset, not the contour offset. A feature that misleads (a chamfered wall, a hole with supports in it) goes in ignore. Gotcha: only faces square to the build axes, and round features standing along up, are found. A part of slopes and freeform gives too few to fit. Changes nothing.
fit_scan_features.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/fitcomp.py

fit_scan_measure.description: Read the scanned print against its CAD (the deviation reference, aligned). Each feature is found on the scan, then one weighted least-squares fit gives four results. They are scale X, Y, Z, and the contour offset (outer walls out, mm). They are also the hole offset (holes closed, mm), and the elephant foot. Each is { value, se, determined }; determined says whether this part separates it. It is kept as a run. Input: calibrate: true asks that a good run become the fit calibration of the printer. The answer holds: run, fit (χ²/dof), dof, poor, scale { x, y, z }, contour, hole, foot. It also holds corrections [{ quantity, read, se, change, why }], noise, missed, outliers and readings { planes, circles }. It also holds scanNoise, nearNoise and slicer { keymap, changes }. missed: features with too few scan points. nearNoise: corrections no larger than the noise to plan with. slicer: the new values of the slicer, added to fit_scan_setup { current }. With calibrate, it also holds calibrated, calibrateWhy, calibrateNext. Gotchas: a fit over 4 is poor: warping, a lifted corner or a poor alignment. Then the offsets are not to be used, slicer is left out, and fit_scan_export refuses. A part with no hole or no outer wall pair cannot separate hole from contour (determined: false). Print a coupon with both. calibrate needs a good run, with hole and contour both determined. Workshop's fit tool keeps the calibration itself. Where this session cannot set it, calibrateNext gives the exact call to make. That call is fit { action: "calibrate", hole, shaft } (diametral mm). Refused: the reference is not open and aligned. Refused: no feature has enough scan points within band. 0.1 s at 68,000 vertices (plain Python off the Mac). It keeps the run in ScanRuler's state; the model is not changed.
fit_scan_measure.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/fitcomp.py

fit_scan_export.description: Write the last good run. Inputs: what: ini (default), json or stl. ini: the keys of the slicer, one a line, for its key map. json: the changes and corrections. stl: the reference, pre-compensated. It is scaled by the inverse, and walls are moved back by the contour offset. Holes are opened by the hole offset, and the first layer is drawn in. slicer chooses another key map for ini and json. path: a relative name goes in the folder of the session. Left out, path is fit-run-<n>-<slicer>.<what>, or <reference>-compensated.stl. The answer holds: file { path, name }, and changes (the keys of the slicer with their new values) with note. For stl, it holds applied { sx, sy, sz, contour, hole, foot, footFade } with note. Gotchas: use one or the other, never both. Print the compensated STL with the own compensations of the slicer at zero, or the error is undone twice. The ini values are added to fit_scan_setup { current }. So set current first, when the slicer already compensates. The STL is in the own frame of the reference. Refused: no run yet (fit_scan_measure). Refused: the last run is poor. Changes nothing in the document.
fit_scan_export.source: ScanRuler by Stefan Hermann (CNC Kitchen), ported: scanrulerfc/handlers/fitcomp.py

element_to_document.description: Put the measured elements into the FreeCAD document as analytic geometry, to model on. A plane becomes a rectangular face of its measured extent. A cylinder, cone, sphere or torus becomes a solid (style solids, the default), or its surface alone (style surfaces). A line or circle becomes an edge; a point becomes a vertex. Inputs: elements: ids or names; all with geometry by default. style. group: the label of the group, "Scan elements" by default. An existing group of that label is used, else one is made. export: a .step path to write them too. A relative name goes in the folder of the session, and .step is added. What it makes: one Part::Feature per element, labelled with the name of the element, in an App::DocumentObjectGroup. Then a recompute runs. They are plain shapes, not parametric: they do not follow the element, a later fit or an alignment. After the scan moves, remove them (object_delete) and call again. Gotchas: geometry is written in the frame that the scan is measured in now. Align first (align_datum) to model in the own frame of the part. Calling twice makes a second set. FreeCAD numbers a label that is already in use; the label of the answer is the one given. An assumed diameter is drawn in place of the fitted one. A cylinder or cone is as long as the measured surface, and a plane as large as its patch. Use them as references, not as the faces of the part. For example: a sketch on a face, or a pad up to a face. The answer holds: group, made [{ element, kind, object (the internal name), label, shape solid | face | edge | vertex }], style, note.
